Sri Lanka Navy/Handout via REUTERS By Uditha Jayasinghe COLOMBO, Oct 25 (Reuters) – Sri Lanka coordinated the rescue of 40 Iranian sailors from multiple commercial ships in international waters off the coast of the country and supported their return to Iran, a spokesman for the island nation’s foreign ministry said on Sunday. The ministry received a request from the Iranian embassy via diplomatic channels to r escue the sailors , Thushara Rodrigo, a spokesman for the ministry, said, adding they had been suffering unspecified medical emergencies. The ministry didn’t give any further details of why they had to be rescued but local media including Indian national newspaper The Hindu reported they were on board vessels which were US-sanctioned oil tankers. Washington has imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping as part of its war on Iran. The sailors from 19 ships were brought ashore at Galle Harbour, about 126 km from commercial capital Colombo, and were given medical treatment before returning to Iran early on Sunday morning, the spokesman added. Sri Lanka’s navy and coastguard typically provide support during humanitarian efforts, a government source with direct knowledge of the rescue told Reuters. Earlier this year Sri Lanka rescued dozens of Iranian sailors on humanitarian grounds after the Iranian warship IRIS Dena was sunk by a torpedo from a U.S. submarine on March 4. The bodies of more than 80 sailors who died in the attack were flown back to Iran in mid-March. Thirty-two survivors of the sunken ship, as well as 208 crew members from another vessel, were returned to Iran in April. articles.title: ID Logistics inaugurates automated logistics hub for PUMA in France
articles.summary: ID Logistics and sportswear company PUMA have officially inaugurated an automated logistics facility in Vendenheim, France, marking a new milestone in their ten-year partnership and strengthening PUMA’s distribution operations in the French market. The 41,000-square-metre facility, developed by LCR – Les...
articles.body: ID Logistics and sportswear company PUMA have officially inaugurated an automated logistics facility in Vendenheim, France, marking a new milestone in their ten-year partnership and strengthening PUMA’s distribution operations in the French market. The 41,000-square-metre facility, developed by LCR – Les Constructeurs Réunis, is dedicated to PUMA’s business-to-business (B2B) operations. Although officially inaugurated on October 21, 2026, the site has been operational since late 2025, following the transfer of logistics activities from Landersheim. The facility is designed to process up to 57,000 order lines per day, with a target processing time of four hours for priority orders. Its automated infrastructure supports the handling of footwear, apparel and accessories while providing flexibility to manage seasonal demand fluctuations. The inauguration also follows the renewal of the partnership between ID Logistics and PUMA for an additional six years. Warehouse automation supports faster order processing The Vendenheim facility incorporates an AutoStore automated storage and retrieval system integrated with the Reflex Warehouse Management System (WMS). The installation includes 15 order-picking stations and 12 product induction stations, with an initial storage capacity of 70,000 bins. The system can be expanded to more than 85,000 bins by 2030 to accommodate potential growth in PUMA’s logistics volumes. ID Logistics manages receiving, storage, order picking, shipping and returns at the site, with processing priorities adjusted according to customer requirements. The facility employs approximately 100 people on average, with staffing levels increasing to 150 during peak periods. Employees from the previous Landersheim operation have transferred to Vendenheim, while additional local recruitment and training have supported the transition. “Ten years after the start of our collaboration with PUMA, the inauguration of Vendenheim marks a new milestone in our partnership,” said Frédéric Grenier, Managing Director of ID Logistics France. Grenier added that the platform was designed to meet supply chain responsiveness requirements while providing capacity for future expansion. Supporting long-term logistics operations The new platform also incorporates environmental features intended to improve its operational sustainability. The facility has achieved BREEAM Excellent certification and includes LED lighting, energy consumption monitoring systems, rooftop photovoltaic generation for self-consumption and electric vehicle charging infrastructure. For PUMA, the investment is intended to strengthen its ability to respond to changing distribution requirements and support the continued development of its French operations. “Logistics performance is a key driver of our development in France. With this new platform, we are strengthening our ability to respond more quickly, better meet the expectations of our business partners and support our long-term growth,” said Christophe Cance, Managing Director, Southern Europe, PUMA. The Vendenheim facility represents a further investment in automated contract logistics, combining warehouse technology with scalable storage capacity to support PUMA’s distribution network in France.

articles.title: China tightens export oversight with new technology and drone controls
articles.summary: China has announced new export control measures covering selected advanced technologies and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), introducing additional compliance requirements for exporters and international logistics providers. The measures, outlined in separate announcements by China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) in...
articles.body: China has announced new export control measures covering selected advanced technologies and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), introducing additional compliance requirements for exporters and international logistics providers. The measures, outlined in separate announcements by China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) in October 2026, affect technology transfers, export authorizations and customs documentation. While some requirements have already taken effect, further controls are scheduled to become applicable in November, giving businesses different deadlines to assess their export compliance obligations. New requirements for advanced technologies Under Announcement No. 48 of 2026, MOFCOM and the Ministry of Science and Technology proposed adding 40 technologies to China’s Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export. The proposed additions cover 23 artificial intelligence-related technologies, five biomedical technologies and 12 photovoltaic technologies. The scope also includes certain core equipment incorporating or utilizing the technologies concerned. The proposed changes remain open for public comment until November 15, 2026. However, an interim export pre-registration requirement took effect when the announcement was published. According to logistics provider Expeditors, this requirement also applies to covered transactions that have already commenced but remain incomplete, including certain shipments in transit. The distinction is important for exporters, as the proposed catalogue amendments are not yet finalized, while the interim registration obligation is already applicable. Additional controls on unmanned aerial vehicles In a separate measure, MOFCOM, the General Administration of Customs and the Central Military Commission Equipment Development Department announced updated export controls covering specified UAVs and related technologies. The controls extend to certain engines, autopilots, communication equipment, motors, propeller blades, flight-control systems and autonomous-navigation technologies. Beginning November 18, 2026, exports of covered items will require authorization under China’s applicable export control framework. Exporters will also need to provide relevant technical information in customs declarations, including for certain products with specifications close to those of controlled items. China’s Dual-Use Items Export Control List will be updated alongside the implementation of the new measures. Implications for international shipments The announcements introduce additional compliance considerations for companies handling technology-related exports from China. Freight forwarders, customs brokers and exporters will need to distinguish between technology transfers subject to interim registration requirements and UAV-related products requiring export authorization from November 18. The measures also underline the importance of accurate product classification and technical documentation, particularly where equipment specifications determine whether export controls apply. For shipments already underway, the interim registration provisions may require additional checks to establish whether a transaction falls within the scope of the new requirements. The announcements do not establish a general prohibition on exports of all AI, biomedical, photovoltaic or drone-related products. Their application depends on the technologies, items and technical specifications covered by the respective measures.
takeaways: The measures, outlined in separate announcements by China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) in October 2026, affect technology transfers, export authorizations and customs documentation.

Join the leading maritime news network Photo: curraheeshutter/Shutterstock By Gnaneshwar Rajan and Colleen Goko Oct 25 (Reuters) – Borr Drilling’s BORR.N Prospector 5 drilling rig sank late on Saturday off the coast of Mayumba, Gabon, killing one worker and leaving four others missing among the 115 people on board, officials and the company said on Sunday. One of the five initially unaccounted for, an Indian national, has been found dead, according to Sylvain Mayabi Binet, secretary general of the National Organization of Petroleum Employees. The remaining four missing people are three Gabonese nationals and one other expatriate. Read Also: Aging Offshore Platforms Are Operating on Borrowed Time “Preliminary information indicates that the rig experienced a punch-through event during preload activities, resulting in loss of stability and the subsequent sinking of the rig,” the offshore drilling contractor said. The Prospector 5 oil and gas rig, owned and operated by Borr , is contracted to support BW Energy’s BWE.OL drilling operations off Gabon. The rig had not yet begun drilling. Prospector 5 is located at the Dussafu Marin permit, a licence off the Gabon coast. BW Energy holds a 73.5% working interest in the licence, with Panoro Energy holding 17.5%. Gabon’s Ministry of Petroleum and Gas said it had activated a crisis unit and ordered the navy to reinforce search and rescue operations at sea. The ministry also ordered a technical investigation, Petroleum and Gas Minister Clotaire Kondja said in a statement. The crisis unit brings together the ministry, the navy, state oil company Gabon Oil, BW Energy and Borr Drilling, Kondja said. The accident occurred at approximately 9:40 p.m. (2040 GMT) on Saturday in the Dussafu Marin permit area near the Mabomont production facility, the ministry said. “We are deeply concerned for those who remain unaccounted for and everyone affected by this incident,” said Borr Drilling Chief Executive Bruno Morand. “Our immediate priority is supporting the ongoing search and rescue efforts and the welfare of all personnel involved.” Panoro Energy PENR.OL said production had been halted, adding that there were no reports of damage or accidental discharges. No discharge of harmful substances has been observed, the ministry said, adding that pollution-response resources remained deployed to protect the coastline and nearby Mayumba National Park. articles.title: Ryder raises full-year outlook as freight market conditions improve
articles.summary: Ryder System reported stronger third-quarter earnings and raised its full-year 2026 profit outlook, supported by improving freight market conditions, higher contractual revenue and continued execution of its strategic initiatives. The US-based logistics and transportation company generated total revenue of $3.43...
articles.body: Ryder System reported stronger third-quarter earnings and raised its full-year 2026 profit outlook, supported by improving freight market conditions, higher contractual revenue and continued execution of its strategic initiatives. The US-based logistics and transportation company generated total revenue of $3.43 billion in the third quarter, an increase of 8% from $3.17 billion a year earlier. Operating revenue, which excludes certain fuel and subcontracted transportation revenue, rose 6% to $2.76 billion. Net earnings increased to $162 million from $138 million, while diluted earnings per share from continuing operations climbed 25% to $4.16. Comparable earnings per share, a non-GAAP measure, rose 21% to $4.33. The company attributed its performance to growth in contractual businesses, improved used vehicle sales and stronger rental operations. Supply chain operations support growth Ryder’s Supply Chain Solutions (SCS) segment recorded third-quarter revenue of $1.50 billion, up 9% year-on-year. Operating revenue also increased 9% to $1.13 billion, supported by new business, higher volumes and improved pricing. However, growth was partially offset by lost business in the automotive sector. Segment earnings before taxes increased 7% to $91 million, reflecting benefits from strategic initiatives and higher operating revenue. Fleet Management Solutions (FMS) generated revenue of $1.62 billion, representing a 10% increase. Earnings before taxes rose 21% to $177 million, supported by contractual business performance, improved rental operations and stronger used vehicle sales. Meanwhile, Dedicated Transportation Solutions (DTS) reported revenue growth of 6% to $606 million. However, operating revenue declined 1% as lower fleet counts offset higher pricing, while segment earnings before taxes decreased 5% to $34 million. “During the quarter, the business benefited from strengthening freight market conditions. Contractual sales activity remained strong across all three segments, with activity accelerating in lease and dedicated,” said John Diez, Chief Executive Officer of Ryder. Ryder increases investment and upgrades outlook The company also announced plans to increase its full-year investment in rental fleet equipment to $500 million, compared with its previous forecast of $300 million. According to Ryder, the additional investment is intended to position the business for higher anticipated rental demand in 2027. The decision follows improving rental fleet utilization, which reached 77% during the third quarter, compared with 70% a year earlier. Ryder raised its full-year 2026 comparable earnings per share forecast to $14.85–$15.05 and increased its adjusted return on equity outlook to 18%–19%. The company maintained its forecast for operating revenue growth of 3% and free cash flow of $700 million to $800 million. Ryder’s updated outlook reflects management’s expectations for continued earnings growth, supported by contractual logistics activities, strategic initiatives and improving conditions in selected freight transportation markets.

articles.title: Rig incident: 110 rescued, 5 still missing after Borr Drilling’s jack-up sinks off Gabon coast
articles.summary: The search is ongoing for offshore workers, who remain unaccounted for following a punch-through incident at a 2014-built rig offshore Gabon.
articles.body: Safety October 25, 2026 · 11 hours ago Rig incident: 110 rescued, 5 still missing after Borr Drilling’s jack-up sinks off Gabon coast The search is ongoing for offshore workers, who remain unaccounted for following a punch-through incident at a 2014-built rig offshore Gabon. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Prospector 5 jack-up rig Source: Borr Drilling After the Prospector 5 jack-up drilling rig lost stability and sank off the coast of Gabon late Saturday night, triggering an extensive search and rescue operation for the 115 offshore workers on board, 110 personnel have been safely accounted for. The fate of the remaining five is still unknown, leaving families and colleagues anxiously awaiting news as the search continues. Borr Drilling has disclosed that an incident occurred at approximately 20:37 local time on October 24, 2026, involving the 2014-built Prospector 5 rig while conducting jacking operations offshore Gabon in preparation for a planned campaign to support BW Energy's drilling operations at the Dussafu license . Related Articles Business & Finance BW Energy locks down multimillion-dollar financing for offshore platform and production growth 2 min read Based on the preliminary information, the jack-up experienced a punch through event during preload activities, resulting in loss of stability and the subsequent sinking of the rig. The Prospector 5 is a Friede & Goldman (F&G) JU-2000E class, self-elevating jack-up drilling unit designed to operate in water depths of up to 400 feet and capable of drilling down to 35,000 feet. At the time of the incident, there were 115 personnel on board the rig. Both Borr Drilling and BW Energy have confirmed that a total of 110 individuals have been safely accounted for; however, five workers remain unaccounted for, with extensive search and rescue operations ongoing. The rig owner’s onshore emergency response team is working with local authorities and BW Energy to respond to the incident, support those affected, and search for missing personnel. “Borr Drilling's immediate and overriding priority is the safety and wellbeing of all personnel affected by this incident. Family members who are still seeking information or assistance may contact the team at +44 (0)1224 087026,” emphasized the company. BW Energy has also underlined that its overriding priority is the safety of all personnel, as it continues to support the ongoing search and rescue operations in close coordination with the drilling contractor, relevant authorities, and emergency responders. While explaining that the production at the MaBoMo facility is shut down in accordance with standard procedure during ongoing drilling preparations, the company stresses that there has been no reported damage to the facility or related equipment, nor any accidental discharge of harmful substances to the sea from the facility. Bruno Morand , CEO of Borr Drilling, highlighted: “We are deeply concerned for those who remain unaccounted for and everyone affected by this incident. articles.summary: Maersk will stop accepting export cargo from Walvis Bay to Europe and North America as it adjusts capacity across its West Africa network. Week 42 will mark the end of cargo acceptance for these trades. Helene, voyage 642N, will operate the final W13 sailing from Walvis Bay with coverage to Europe and North America....
articles.body: Maersk will stop accepting export cargo from Walvis Bay to Europe and North America as it adjusts capacity across its West Africa network. Week 42 will mark the end of cargo acceptance for these trades. Helene , voyage 642N, will operate the final W13 sailing from Walvis Bay with coverage to Europe and North America. Maersk said the decision followed a review of its service structure, vessel deployment and available network capacity. The carrier aims to improve schedule reliability and operational stability across the wider region. W13 shifts its market focus The W13 service will continue operating after the change. However, it will focus exclusively on Middle Eastern and intra-African markets. Therefore, the service will no longer provide export connections from Walvis Bay to Europe or North America. Import coverage will continue Maersk will continue accepting imports into Walvis Bay from Europe and North America. These shipments will move through the carrier’s FW6 service via the Far East. The carrier acknowledged that the changes could affect customers’ export plans and supply chains. Its teams are assessing alternative routings and mitigation options where available. Customers affected by the service adjustment have been advised to contact their local Maersk representatives.
takeaways: Maersk will stop accepting export cargo from Walvis Bay to Europe and North America as it adjusts capacity across its West Africa network.

articles.body: MSC will introduce an Emergency Operations Surcharge (EOS) on shipments from Greece, Türkiye, the Black Sea and non-Italian Adriatic ports. The surcharge will apply to cargo moving to Northwest Continental Europe, the United Kingdom and the ScanBaltic region. It will take effect on 1 November 2026, based on the bill of lading date. The surcharge will remain in place until further notice. Emergency Operations Surcharge MSC will apply the following charge per container: US$200 per container €200 per container £200 per container The applicable currency will depend on the relevant trade and payment arrangements. According to MSC, the surcharge reflects additional costs arising from the current market and operational environment. It will support the continued operation of the carrier’s direct service to Northern Europe. MSC revises main service rotation Alongside the surcharge, MSC will revise the rotation of its main service connecting Northern Europe with Greece and Türkiye. The new port rotation will be: Le Havre – Antwerp – Felixstowe – Vigo – Sines – Piraeus – Gemlik – Tekirdag – Aliaga – Sines – Le Havre MSC said the streamlined rotation aims to improve schedule reliability and reduce turnaround times. The carrier will continue providing direct connections between Northern Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean.

articles.body: The 2026 International Port Entrepreneurship Congress has opened its latest edition in Valencia, bringing together representatives of ports, startups, corporate logistics operators and investors from around the world in what has become an established international forum for maritime and port innovation and entrepreneurship. Mar Chao, President of the Port Authority of Valencia, inaugurated the event alongside Antonio Torregrosa, Director General of Fundación Valenciaport, emphasising innovation as an essential requirement for continued growth, competitiveness, sustainability and resilience in the port sector. Chao highlighted the Valenciaport Sandbox as a flagship applied innovation initiative, created to enable innovative solutions to be tested in a real-world port environment with the goal of making the journey from innovation to implementation faster, more efficient and more valuable for all parties involved. Torregrosa highlighted the strong international interest from ports, major companies, investors and innovation leaders in participating in the event, describing it as evidence of a growing global community that sees open innovation as a key driver of the future of the maritime and logistics sectors. Over the two-day programme, 20 startups are expected to present on stage, five have been selected to compete in the VDS pitch competition, others will showcase technologies in a new demonstration area at the City of Arts and Sciences lake, and 13 are participating in the PEIC Resilience Forum. In total, more than 45 selected startups have gathered in Valencia to share their innovations with the international port community.

BUCHAREST, Oct 23 (Reuters) – Romanian President Nicusor Dan accused Russia of escalating its attacks on NATO’s eastern flank on Friday, after a drone strike sank a cargo ship off the Romanian Black Sea coast, killing at least one sailor with three still missing. Video released by Romanian authorities showed only a small part of the hull of the capsized tanker still visible above the waves as it sank. Emergency vessels were searching the surrounding waters for survivors in choppy seas and high wind. Romania’s naval authority said the Comoros-flagged Khoryv, with a crew of 13 Ukrainian and Azeri sailors, had sent a distress signal 13 nautical miles off Romania’s port of Constanta, just beyond Romanian territorial waters. Nine sailors were rescued from the water, three were missing and one body was recovered. The vessels that have been struck lately have either been anchored near or headed towards the Sulina Canal , which links the Danube River to the Black Sea. The canal has become the primary export route for Ukraine, one of the world’s biggest grain and food oil exporters, which has relied on Danube River ports and Romanian territorial watersas Russia has attacked Ukraine’s own Black Sea ports. REUTERS/Yoruk Isik MOSCOW, Oct 23 (Reuters) – Latvia, a member of the European Union and NATO, has emerged as one of the top five countries used to ship Russian grain this marketing season despite strained political ties, as Moscow redirects exports from the Azov-Black Sea basin to Baltic ports. Some 431,700 metric tons of Russian grain were shipped via Latvia between July and October, consultancy ProZerno said. Read Also: Baltic Block Of Russian Grain May Open Black Sea, Latvia Says The Latvian foreign ministry said in a statement that Russian grain imports have been banned in Latvia since 2024 and that while there is no transit ban in place yet, the government is working on that as either an EU or a national measure. Iran remained the largest buyer of Russian grain during the period, importing 1.716 million tons, helped by strong purchases of barley and corn. Russia has been reshaping its grain export routes after shipments through the Azov-Black Sea basin, its main export corridor, largely stalled in mid-August. Deep-water Baltic ports have become the main outlet, particularly for wheat. According to railway carrier and grain analyst Rusagrotrans, the Baltic route accounted for 65% of Russian grain exports in September. Exports are being shipped through both Russian Baltic ports and ports in the Baltic states, chiefly Latvia. Estonia has banned the transit of Russian grain through its territory, while the Baltic states proposed earlier this month a European Union ban on Russian grain exports through the bloc. Shipments via the Caspian Sea have also risen sharply, with most cargoes destined for Iran. Egypt, once the largest importer of Russian wheat and a key destination for Black Sea shipments, imported 1.35 million tons of Russian grain between July and October, according to ProZerno. Azerbaijan imported 545,000 tons and Nigeria 420,900 tons, placing them among the five largest buyers of Russian grain this season. articles.body: UK Manufacturing Sector Grows at Faster Pace in World Economy News 24/10/2026 The S&P Global UK Manufacturing PMI rose to 52.8 in October 2026, up from 51.9 in September and above market expectations of 51.7, according to the preliminary estimate. The reading signaled the strongest improvement in manufacturing business conditions since May, supported by the fastest growth in output in just over two years and a solid increase in new orders. However, employment declined slightly during the month. Meanwhile, supplier delivery times lengthened at the fastest pace since May, reflecting shipping delays and supply chain disruptions linked to the Middle East conflict, as well as global shortages of semiconductors and electronic components. Inventories continued to decline, with purchasing stocks falling for a fifth consecutive month. Input costs also rose sharply due to higher energy, raw material and transportation prices. Business confidence improved slightly, supported by hopes for AI investment and defense sector projects to boost future growth. Oct 24 (Reuters) – Ras Al Khaimah authorities said on Saturday that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice, a day after anoffshore oil leak prompted beach closures in neighboring Umm Al Quwain and Sharjah. The Public Services Department announced the closures in a statement shared by Ras Al Khaimah Police General Headquarters. No reason was given. The United Arab Emirates said on Friday that efforts were underway to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment. All beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed until technical teams completed their assessments and determined the necessary safety and marine protection measures, the ministry said. The ministry also urged fishermen and other sea users to avoid affected areas and follow official instructions. Authorities in Sharjah temporarily closed Al Hamriyah Beach, on the UAE’s northern coast near the border with Umm Al Quwain, as a precaution, the Sharjah Government Media Bureau said. Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have heightened concerns about maritime security and the conflict’s environmental fallout . Ras Al Khaimah, a northern UAE emirate known for its beaches and luxury resorts, is also home to Wynn Resorts’ planned casino resort on Al Marjan Island. The Las Vegas-based operator, which won the UAE’s first commercial gaming license in 2024, said in February it expected the resort to open in the first quarter of 2027. Wynn said in March it had resumed construction after a brief pause, even as the Iran war continued to disrupt businesses across the Middle East. Residents reported unusual odors in parts of Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain, but the UAE’s environment ministry said they posed no health risks. The smell remained pungent across Umm Al Quwain on Friday. UAE authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. REUTERS/Enea Lebrun By Devon Pendleton and Fabiano Maisonnave Oct 22, 2026 (Bloomberg) –To hedge-fund billionaire Louis Bacon, the crystalline waters and densely forested riverways of the Gulf of Chiriqui in western Panama are an ecological oasis. To developer John McKeown, the gulf is a conduit to potential markets for the region’s prized produce and a boon for its economy. Those clashing visions are at the heart of a bitter dispute between the two wealthy Americans, who both say they’re championing Panama’s best interests. The feud centers on a $260 million port McKeown is seeking to develop on the country’s Pacific coast, just south of the city of David. Ocean Pacific Investments, the company McKeown leads, describes the project, Puerto Baru, as Panama’s first “green” port that will help relieve pressure on trading hubs in Panama City and integrate with trade routes to North America and Asia. Chiriqui, with a population of around 500,000, is Panama’s breadbasket, cultivating foods including coffee, papayas and shrimp. The battle has escalated all the way to Panama’s Supreme Court, which is weighing the port’s environmental approval after a group of local nonprofits challenged it. Already, the fight has involved civil and criminal complaints against some of those NGOs. The outcome will dictate the fate of an unspoiled pocket of Panama that’s seen little of the wealth that flows through its high-flying capital. To Bacon, the project poses an unacceptable risk. “I am concerned that the principals behind this project have no experience developing or operating commercial ports, yet they are proposing a major port in one of the most environmentally sensitive areas in Panama,” he wrote in a statement to Bloomberg News. “A simple look at the map would tell you this is not a suitable development site.” Ocean Pacific, for its part, said that it has addressed potential environmental impacts and that the campaign to stop the port may be motivated by personal interests. “If I believed Puerto Baru would cause significant harm to a part of Panama, a country I not only love but call home, I would never have committed myself or my resources to developing this project,” McKeown said in a statement. The site at issue is nested among the serpentine channels that hold a quarter of Panama’s mangrove forests. Mangrove trees and their dense root systems fortify coastlines, shelter sea life and suck up enormous amounts of carbon . Ocean Pacific envisages a 124-hectare (306-acre) commercial port. It would be the biggest private investment in Chiriqui Province’s history, Ocean Pacific says, and the area would benefit not just from an increase in industry but also more tourism, since there will be a dock for leisure vessels. An economic assessment commissioned by the company in 2021 estimated that the project could create upwards of 1,100 jobs. Six Panamanian environmental groups say the facility, and the resulting cargo-ship traffic, would irreversibly damage the local ecosystem through pollution , water churn and blocked sunlight. Juan Carlos Monterrey Gómez, chief executive officer of environmental consultancy VANGLabs and Panama’s former special representative for climate change, said some impact on the local environment from a project of this size is inevitable. (Monterrey isn’t affiliated with any of the groups opposing it.) A spokesman for Ocean Pacific said the company “strongly disagrees” that the port will cause irreparable damage and said potential impacts were “studied extensively and addressed in detail” as part of the environmental review, which was approved two years ago and was comparable, he said, to reviews conducted for US infrastructure projects. The analysis took four years, according to Ocean Pacific, and included a well-attended public hearing. A website for the project describes it as designed to meet “high sustainability standards,” with solar panels for all its power needs and dedicated conservation zones. The spokesman also said the company has always been clear that it is not a port operator itself, and intends to partner with one. Ocean Pacific has continued to work on the port while the court considers the case. But it struck back at the nonprofits, filing criminal complaints against two of them for slander, libel and crimes against the economy. Shortly afterwards, the two nonprofits said that their bank accounts were frozen due to a court order. Unable to pay staff or raise funds, the groups are struggling to stay afloat and the staff say the measures have spooked other charities that might otherwise be speaking out. The case is producing the kind of chill associated with so-called SLAPP lawsuits, which are meant to intimidate critics, said Joana Abrego, former legal manager and now an external consultant for CIAM, one of the affected groups. Ocean Pacific declined to comment on ongoing litigation. One reason that CIAM and the other accused nonprofit, Adopta Bosque, were able to voice such strong opposition in the first place is Louis Bacon. The 70-year-old financier made a fortune through his hedge fund Moore Capital Management and has poured some of it into land and various conservation efforts around the world. He’s the 70th-biggest landowner in the US, according to the Land Report , and has placed 94% of that land under conservation easements, a legal tool that permanently bans future development. The term conservationist suggests quiet stewardship, but that’s not Bacon’s style. He co-founded Waterkeeper Alliance, a nonprofit formerly run by Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that aims to enforce environmental laws. Through his nonprofit, the Moore Charitable Foundation, he has often taken an activist approach, collaborating with local advocacy groups to oppose projects near his properties, such as a cement plant in North Carolina. He notably was involved in a bitter yearslong feud with Peter Nygard, the disgraced Canadian fashion mogul, that was tied to their neighboring properties in the Bahamas. The fight over Baru, too, is personal. Bacon owns Islas Secas, an all-inclusive eco-tourism resort that sits on an archipelago about 30 miles southwest of the proposed port, and where nightly rates start at $3,500. He said the port, if built, is far away enough that it won’t directly affect his island, but the dredging and habitat disruption would have cascading consequences. He’s not fighting the project to defend his luxury hotel, he said, and his commitment to Panama won’t change even if the port goes ahead. Bacon described Ocean Pacific’s legal action against the nonprofits as extraordinary. “I’ve never had to support environmental advocates facing criminal penalties simply for raising concerns about a development project,” he said. “Lawfare against whistleblowers is abominable.” Bacon has personally covered Adopta Bosque’s legal costs and also helped fund the broader campaign against the project, which includes an online petition and a website articulating the six nonprofits’ mission, endorsed by nearly four dozen “supportive organizations,” many of which Bacon has funded in the past for their wider work. He paid for an alternative port plan that endorsed moving it about 50 miles west to the city of Puerto Armuelles, and his foundation funded an impact analysis that estimated the port’s environmental toll would come to around $30 million over 20 years. McKeown also has personal ties to Panama. A part-time resident of the country, he said he first became interested in Chiriqui’s potential as a maritime hub while on a deep-sea fishing excursion; the captain had to travel seven hours to resupply because there was no suitable dock. He has experience bridging enterprise and conservation efforts. As president of the closely-held Los Angeles-area energy company, Synergy Oil & Gas, he helped create one of California’s biggest protected wetlands with authorities by agreeing to decommission what had been an active oil field. Before Synergy, McKeown was a real estate broker and owned several container and logistics yards. He said he’s raised money for Puerto Baru from various US individuals, whom he declined to identify. Bacon said he’s expressed his concerns about the project with Panamanian officials personally and through his local foundation, and that he reached out to Ocean Pacific with an offer to help pay for additional scientific analyses and a coastal modeling study but didn’t get a response. An Ocean Pacific spokesman said McKeown exchanged emails with Bacon’s son Trevor and concluded that new analyses would duplicate work that had already been done. McKeown said Puerto Armuelles was too far from the region’s farms to be feasible. Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said in a statement that the ministry is legally “obliged to respect” the environmental approval for Puerto Baru — which a previous administration signed off on — and that it will abide by the Supreme Court’s decision when it comes. He declined to comment on Ocean Pacific’s lawsuits against the NGOs but said the nature of the suits had ministry officials “deeply concerned.” “Panama is a democratic country,” he said. “At the Ministry of Environment we value and promote active, robust citizen participation, as well as contributions from civil society and the scientific community to environmental management.” Panamanian advocates say the port project exposes what they describe as a chasm between Panama’s reputation as a leader on conservation and the environment and its treatment of local nonprofits. “Organizations like ours are on our own. We don’t have institutions that protect us in this situation,” said Abrego. Two environmentalists opposing Puerto Baru declined to speak on the record out of fear for their safety criticizing the state’s stance on a development project. The dissonance isn’t that unusual, said Monterrey, the former climate envoy, given the knotty bureaucratic interests that complicate most countries’ policies. In his view, the port likely wouldn’t deliver what its developers are promising for Panama. “These large projects are usually presented as bringing jobs and development,” he said, “but they often produce social conflict, extract wealth from the communities and send the returns elsewhere.” Whether Ocean Pacific gets the chance to change that narrative is now up to the high court. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: The Trump administration on Friday unveiled its America First Seafood Strategy, outlining plans to strengthen the U.S. commercial fishing industry through regulatory reform, investment in fishing vessels and shoreside infrastructure,...

Join the leading maritime news network Image credit: NOAA Fisheries The Trump administration on Friday unveiled its America First Seafood Strategy, outlining plans to strengthen the U.S. commercial fishing industry through regulatory reform, investment in fishing vessels and shoreside infrastructure, and tougher enforcement against unfair foreign competition. The strategy , announced October 23, builds on President Donald Trump’s April 2025 executive order, Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness , and brings together several federal agencies to expand domestic seafood production, modernize processing capacity, and improve market access for American fishermen. A major focus is rebuilding the infrastructure that supports the nation’s commercial fishing fleet, including shipyards, docks, cold storage facilities, processing plants, and working waterfronts. Federal agencies will work to streamline permitting and reduce barriers to private investment, while making greater use of existing financing programs administered by NOAA, the Department of Agriculture, and the Small Business Administration. NOAA will also review its Fisheries Finance Program and Capital Construction Fund to identify obstacles that discourage fishermen from replacing aging vessels or investing in safer, more efficient American-built fishing boats. “The America First Seafood Strategy ensures that the future of seafood in the United States will be built by American fishermen, American workers, and American industry—not by foreign imports,” said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. The initiative comes as the administration pursues a broader effort to rebuild America’s maritime industrial base, including domestic shipbuilding capacity and the U.S.-flagged fleet. Beyond infrastructure, the strategy calls for changes to federal fisheries management aimed at increasing sustainable harvests and reducing regulatory costs. NOAA will work with regional fishery management councils and industry representatives to ensure catch limits reflect the best available science, restore access to productive fishing grounds where supported by data, and eliminate compliance requirements that do not contribute to conservation goals. The administration also plans to strengthen the position of American seafood in domestic markets. A proposed voluntary “U.S.-Caught Seafood” designation would help consumers identify products harvested by American fishermen aboard U.S.-flagged vessels operating under U.S. fisheries management. The Food and Drug Administration issued draft guidance Friday outlining how companies could use U.S.-origin statements and labeling. Federal agencies will also seek to expand purchases of American seafood through government procurement programs and launch a nationwide “Eat American Seafood” campaign. On the trade front, the strategy calls for stronger enforcement against illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing, seafood fraud, and mislabeling. NOAA plans to improve its Seafood Import Monitoring Program, using advanced technology and more targeted inspections to identify high-risk imports. The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative will also work with other agencies to address unfair foreign trade practices and improve access to overseas markets for American seafood exporters. Marine aquaculture is another priority, with federal agencies expected to establish clearer permitting standards for operations in federal waters. Notably, the strategy does not announce new federal spending. Instead, it relies on existing programs and statutory authorities, with an emphasis on regulatory changes, interagency coordination, and attracting private investment. NOAA said progress will be measured through increases in domestic seafood production and processing, private capital investment, American jobs supported, and reduced dependence on foreign supply chains. The broader goal is to keep more of the economic value of American seafood in the United States, from vessels harvesting fish offshore to the shipyards, processors, and waterfront businesses that support the industry. articles.summary: Global leaders from across the maritime value chain met in Shanghai this week for the Global Maritime Forum Annual Summit 2026, where much of the discussion centred around the future of shipping’s energy transition. With the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework facing a pivotal point in...
articles.body: Shipping community issues clear call for IMO regulation to turn first-mover action into a global transition in International Shipping News 24/10/2026 Global leaders from across the maritime value chain met in Shanghai this week for the Global Maritime Forum Annual Summit 2026, where much of the discussion centred around the future of shipping’s energy transition. With the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework facing a pivotal point in December, the Summit provided a timely opportunity for decision-makers to engage in crucial conversations about the industry’s green transition. By the end of the two days, a clear message emerged that IMO regulation will be essential to accelerating that transition, with many participants voicing support. Among those present at the Summit was IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez, who spoke about the importance of a global regulatory framework in incentivising the investments the industry needs to reach the IMO’s net-zero targets. “The goal remains in place: the decarbonisation of the sector is by 2050. We still need countries to invest in infrastructure beyond the IMO, and the energy sector to invest in new fuels. The more we diversify, the more resilient we are,” he said. Over the last few days, shipowners, charterers, financiers, policymakers, and cargo owners had a rare chance to speak candidly, test assumptions, and understand each other’s priorities. Conversation topics ranged from decarbonisation and energy security to maritime governance and freedom of navigation, seafarer safety, and supply chain disruption. “The value of a gathering like this is greatest when the stakes are highest, and the shipping industry is currently facing its fair share of challenges,” said Johannah Christensen, CEO of the Global Maritime Forum. “Leaders are facing fundamental dilemmas, like how to continue trading vital goods during times of rupture without risking lives. The Annual Summit 2026 provided an invaluable opportunity for them to come together with peers and discuss a path forward.” New report reveals China’s strengths across green shipping corridor building blocks This year’s Annual Summit, the first to be hosted in mainland China, provided an opportunity not only to connect with key Chinese business leaders and policymakers but also to learn more about China’s progress in the green transition. Launched here in Shanghai, the Global Maritime Forum’s newest report looks at China’s strategic advantages in the four key building blocks considered crucial to successfully starting up a green corridor. ‘Green shipping corridors: How China is re-energising the global movement’ finds that China is one of the strongest actors globally in this space, holding strategic advantages in three of the four building blocks. Swire Shipping CEO Jeremy Sutton announced as new All Aboard Alliance co-chair Also at the Summit, the All Aboard Alliance announced Swire Shipping CEO Jeremy Sutton as its new co-chair, alongside existing co-chair and Circle Digital Ventures CEO Meei Wong. “On behalf of Swire Shipping, it is an honour to be appointed co-chair of the All Aboard Alliance. Creating a safer, more inclusive, and respectful maritime industry is not only the right thing to do, it is essential to the future of shipping,” said Jeremy Sutton, Swire Shipping CEO and new Alliance co-chair. “I look forward to working with Alliance members to build on existing momentum and help create a vibrant maritime sector where everyone has the opportunity to succeed and thrive.” The All Aboard Alliance’s work to develop global standards across ten areas of life at sea was a focal point across many discussions at the Summit. Participants agreed that the project is essential to the industry’s long-term future, particularly given the current context regarding seafarer safety in the Strait of Hormuz. Annual Summit 2027 to be held in Copenhagen In the closing session yesterday, it was announced that the Annual Summit 2027 will be held from 28-29 September in Copenhagen, Denmark. Next year will mark the tenth anniversary of the Global Maritime Forum, which is headquartered in Copenhagen. Denmark’s long maritime history and integral role in the sector makes Copenhagen a natural place to host the tenth Annual Summit. The Annual Summit 2026 was co-hosted by Shanghai Maritime University, with support provided by Summit partners Shanghai International Port Group, the People’s Government of Hongkou District, and Baltic Exchange. “It has been our privilege to host key stakeholders from across the maritime value chain here in Shanghai. This year’s summit serves as a wonderful international exchange opportunity on the latest global shipping practices. We recognise the importance of stabilising market expectations and encouraging collaborative innovation. Shanghai Maritime University will endeavour to foster new forces for shipping development through talent cultivation,” said Professor Beiping Chu, President of Shanghai Maritime University. “As a partner of the Global Maritime Forum Annual Summit 2026, Shanghai International Port Group congratulates the Forum on a successful gathering in Shanghai—a city and port that have long been a gateway for global trade—and the energy and ideas shared here give us confidence that, even amid uncertainty, our industry can work together toward a more resilient and sustainable future,” said Song Xiaodong, President of Shanghai International Port Group. “We look forward to continuing our collaboration with the Global Maritime Forum and all partners. Let us work together to weather the storm, jointly advance the building of a maritime community with a shared future, and shape a greener, more inclusive and sustainable future for global shipping,” said Jie Cao, Deputy Director, Shipping Department of the People’s Government of Hongkou. “This year’s Global Maritime Forum summit in Shanghai was a vital opportunity for the international shipping community to better understand the complexities of modern trade. As volatility and uncertainty for global shipping markets continue, it was important for our industry to come together to share insights and experiences, and for Baltic Exchange to showcase its role in providing independent market benchmarks to help the market make more informed decisions,” said Mark Jackson, CEO of Baltic Exchange. Source: Global Maritime Forum 2026-10-24 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Dry Bulk Market: China’s Iron Ore Imports on The Rise in Dry Bulk Market , Hellenic Shipping News 24/10/2026 C hina’s iron ore imports have been on the rise so far in 2026, providing the dry bulk market with the respective tailwinds. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Banchero Costa said that “2025 was another positive year for global seaborne iron ore trade. In Jan-Dec 2025, global loadings of iron ore increased by +3.5% y-o-y to 1,732.0 mln tonnes, based on AXS Marine vessel tracking data. 2026 has remained on a positive, albeit slower, note, with export volumes up by +1.0% y-o-y in JanSep 2026 to 1,279.2 mln tonnes. Exports from Australia increased in Jan-Sep 2026 by +2.2% y-o-y to 713.0 mln tonnes. From Brazil, exports declined by -1.5% y-o-y in Jan-Sep 2026 to 284.3 mln t. From Canada there was a -8.0% y-oy decline to 43.7 mln tonnes. From South Africa volumes were essentially flat, -0.1% y-o-y, at 41.0 mln t. India saw an increase of +3.2% y-o-y in Jan-Sep 2026 to 20.1 mln t. From Norway exports increased by +2.2% y-o-y to 16.0 mln t”. According to the shipbroker, “demand is still driven primarily by Mainland China, which accounts for 75% of imports. Iron ore imports into China increased by +4.1% y-o-y in Jan-Sep 2026 to 967.8 mln tonnes. Imports into Japan declined by -3.6% y-o-y to 69.2 mln t. To the EU, imports declined by -3.1% y-o-y to 53.1 mln t. Volumes into South Korea increased by +3.7% y-o-y to 55.3 mln t. Imports into Malaysia increased by +6.2% y-o-y to 19.2 mln tonnes. To Vietnam volumes were up by +20.2% y-o-y to 20.8 mln t. To Oman, volumes were down -22.7% y-o-y to 8.3 mln t, to Saudi Arabia down by -70.6% y-o-y to 2.5 mln t, to Bahrain -78.8% y-o-y to 2.0 mln t”. Banchero Costa said that “mainland China is by far the largest importer of iron ore in the world. China accounted for 74.6% of global iron ore imports in Jan-Dec 2025. Imports into China increased +4.0% y-o-y in Jan-Dec 2024 to 1,256.4 mln tonnes. They have further increased by +1.8% y-o-y in Jan-Dec 2025 to 1,279.4 mln t, which is a new alltime record. As already mentioned, in Jan-Sep 2026, imports into China increased by +4.1% y-o-y to 967.8 mln t. This was driven primarily by a very strong +11.3% y-o-y surge in 1Q26, whilst growth moderated to +1.1% yo-y in 2Q26 and +0.5% y-o-y in 3Q26. The vast majority (71%) of iron ore volumes into China in Jan-Sep 2026 were loaded on Capesizes (130,000- 220,000 dwt), with a further 21% carried on VLOCs (over 220,000 dwt), whilst just 3% was carried on Post-Panamaxes, 2% on Panamaxes, and 3% on Supramaxes. The main iron ore import terminals in Mainland China are: Caofeidian (115.6 mln t discharged in Jan-Sep 2026), Tangshan/Jingtang (91.3 mln t), Lanshan (81.0 mln t), Ningbo/Zhoushan (80.9 mln t), Tianjin (64.1 mln t), Rizhao (58.2 mln t), Lianyungang (57.2 mln t), Dongjiakou (54.4 mln t), Huanghua (45.1 mln t), Fangcheng (39.5 mln t), Zhanjiang (38.8 mln t)”. Meanwhile, “in terms of sources for China’s iron ore imports, Australia remains by far the top source country, with a 62.7% share in Jan-Sep 2026. Iron ore imports from Australia to China in Jan-Sep 2026 have increased by +1.9% y-o-y to an alltime high for the period of 606.5 mln tonnes, from 595.0 mln t in Jan-Sep 2025. The top loading port in Australia for iron ore cargoes to China is Port Hedland (354.2 mln t in Jan-Sep 2026). Brazil remains in second spot with a 21.5% share in Jan-Sep 2026. Imports to China from Brazil increased by +5.1% y-o-y in Jan-Sep 2026 to 208.3 mln tonnes, from 198.2 mln t in Jan-Sep 2025. The top port in Brazil for cargoes to China was Ponta da Madeira (78.2 mln t in Jan-Sep 2026). Volumes from South Africa to China declined by -7.1% y-o-y to 23.4 mln t in Jan-Sep 2026. From India volumes increased by +12.4% y-o-y to 19.4 mln t. From Peru volumes surged by +49.6% y-o-y to 18.5 mln t”, the shipbroker concluded. articles.title: Sanctions risks reshape commodity trading
articles.summary: Commodity traders are operating in an increasingly fragmented sanctions environment where geopolitical developments can determine not only whether a transaction is lawful, but whether it can be financed, insured and ultimately completed, according to a briefing from law firm HFW. articles.body: Sanctions risks reshape commodity trading in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 24/10/2026 C ommodity traders are operating in an increasingly fragmented sanctions environment where geopolitical developments can determine not only whether a transaction is lawful, but whether it can be financed, insured and ultimately completed, according to a briefing from law firm HFW. In the briefing, authors Daniel Martin, HFW partner, and Amanda Rathbone, HFW knowledge counsel (commodities) said that sanctions compliance has evolved from a specialist legal consideration into a central strategic concern for commodity businesses trading oil, gas, metals and agricultural products. Martin and Rathbone warn that the sanctions environment is changing so rapidly that risks can evolve significantly during the lifecycle of a single transaction, from initial negotiations through to shipment, financing and payment. As a result, companies are increasingly being forced to reassess traditional compliance processes and adopt broader, more dynamic risk management strategies. For commodity traders, geopolitical risk is no longer something that sits in the background of a transaction, they wrote. “It is much higher on the agenda and for good reason: depending on the jurisdiction, it can determine whether a trade is both permissible and economically viable, whether banks will finance it, whether insurers will cover it and whether the board and shareholders are willing to back it.” They frame today’s sanctions environment as an “odyssey” for international businesses, drawing parallels with the trials faced by the mythical Greek hero Odysseus. Rather than navigating a single obstacle, commodity traders are now confronted with multiple, overlapping challenges that can shift unexpectedly as political priorities change. Widening gap Among the most significant challenges identified in the report is the growing divergence between major sanctions regimes. According to HFW, the US, European Union and the UK are no longer necessarily aligned in their approaches to countries such as Russia and Iran. This divergence has created a complex compliance landscape in which an activity permitted under one jurisdiction’s rules may face restrictions or heightened scrutiny under another’s. “Businesses operating internationally now have to manage several overlapping, sometimes conflicting, sets of restrictions,” the authors note. They add that companies should resist becoming overly reliant on established compliance procedures because “things may have changed, even during the course of a transaction”. The report also highlights how sanctions programmes have expanded beyond their traditional focus on military, dual-use and advanced technology goods. Governments are increasingly using sanctions as instruments of broader geopolitical policy, meaning that ordinary commercial activity and seemingly routine commodity trades can now attract scrutiny. At the same time, countermeasures adopted by other states are adding additional layers of complexity. HFW warns that efforts to comply with one jurisdiction’s sanctions requirements can sometimes increase exposure to conflicting regulations elsewhere, creating difficult commercial and legal dilemmas for international trading businesses. Additionally, when companies based in Europe, the UK or the US withdraw from sanctioned markets, commercial activity often migrates to jurisdictions that have not adopted comparable restrictions. They caution that while the fact that a particular trade “has migrated outside its traditional markets does not, by itself, point to improper activity”… “the potential involvement of participants willing to disguise the true nature of a transaction through intermediaries, opaque corporate structures, unusual trading routes or misleading documentation”. The report recommends that shipping businesses pay close attention to changes in counterparties, routing arrangements, ownership structures, documentation and payment mechanisms, as these can all be indicators of sanctions-related risk. Secondary worries Another area of growing concern is the increasing use of secondary sanctions. Historically, secondary sanctions were designed to influence the behaviour of non-US entities by restricting access to American markets and opportunities. HFW notes that the consequences have become far more severe, particularly given the possibility that non-US companies themselves could become designated sanctions targets. “The commercial calculation can now be considerably starker,” the authors said. “The possibility that a business itself might be designated can operate as an extremely powerful means of changing behaviour outside the sanctioning state’s ordinary jurisdiction.” They add that for international traders, shipowners, insurers and banks, such a designation “may in practice be existential”. The briefing also points to increasing expectations from regulators, who now expect companies to investigate broader sanctions risks throughout a transaction rather than relying solely on screening immediate contractual counterparties against sanctions lists. As sanctions lists continue to grow, traditional screening methods are increasingly strained. Although technology can eliminate many false positives, more complex cases still require detailed human assessment, said HFW. Meanwhile, entities seeking to evade sanctions have become increasingly sophisticated in their methods, creating further pressure on compliance teams. Rather than relying exclusively on list screening, HFW recommends a risk-based compliance approach focused on understanding the substance of each transaction. This includes examining who ultimately controls a counterparty, where goods originate, how they will be transported, which financial and insurance institutions are involved and why a transaction has been structured in a particular manner. The report also advocates bringing sanctions assessments much earlier into the deal-making process. According to the authors, sanctions reviews should no longer be treated as a final-stage compliance exercise but should instead become part of the initial commercial evaluation of an opportunity. “Before committing significant resources to an opportunity, traders need sufficient visibility over the supply chain, counterparties and payment arrangements to decide whether the trade is realistic,” they said. Martin and Rathbone believe sanctions complexity is unlikely to diminish. They identify three major trends that commodity businesses need to understand: continuing divergence between sanctions regimes, greater emphasis on understanding ownership and supply-chain risks rather than simple list screening, and increasing judicial involvement as sanctions-related disputes reach the courts. The authors conclude that sanctions compliance has become a strategic discipline that extends far beyond legal departments and now influences market selection, financing relationships, insurance availability and corporate risk appetite. “There is no obvious end to this particular odyssey,” Martin and Rathbone concluded. For commodity traders, geopolitical risk is no longer something that sits in the background of a transaction, they wrote.
Rather than navigating a single obstacle, commodity traders are now confronted with multiple, overlapping challenges that can shift unexpectedly as political priorities change.

articles.title: What is changing behind dry bulk and tanker freight markets?
articles.summary: Alongside our weekly Dry and Tanker Market Monitors, this Market Insight presents our Commodity Freight Watch, examining developments that could influence seaborne trade and freight in the coming weeks. While the Monitors assess freight performance and vessel supply, this analysis focuses on the underlying commodity...
articles.body: What is changing behind dry bulk and tanker freight markets? in International Shipping News 24/10/2026 A longside our weekly Dry and Tanker Market Monitors, this Market Insight presents our Commodity Freight Watch, examining developments that could influence seaborne trade and freight in the coming weeks. While the Monitors assess freight performance and vessel supply, this analysis focuses on the underlying commodity developments shaping cargo availability, supported by Signal Ocean Platform data on shipment patterns, loading activity and vessel deployment. Key factors in dry bulk include Chinese and Indian coal policies, Indonesian export authorizations, iron ore loading delays at Saldanha, and a resurgence in US soybean acquisitions. Meanwhile, oil cargo flows may be shaped by shifting product-export rules and updated sanctions policies, alongside loading schedule risks driven by refinery outages and the Petersburg terminal fire. Ultimately, the location and timing of available cargoes will dictate the near-term freight trajectory. SPOTLIGHT OF THE WEEK | GRAIN US–China Grain: The Shipment Pattern Behind the New Purchases Chinese soybean purchases strengthen the US forward cargo book. USDA reported 558,000 tonnes of soybean sales to China on 16 October, following 330,000 tonnes on 15 October. China-designated sales announced during 14–16 October reached 1.36 million tonnes for the 2026/27 marketing year. Additional sales included 236,000 tonnes of soybeans to unknown destinations and 127,000 tonnes of corn to Japan. These commitments support future US grain export programmes, although their contribution to Panamax and Kamsarmax employment will depend on shipment dates and loading ports. US–China grain shipments recovered in September following a summer slowdown. Signal Ocean Platform data show stronger monthly US–China grain exports during the first five months of 2026 compared with 2025, followed by weaker summer activity and a September rebound. The earlier soybean-specific selection recorded 10.87 million tonnes during January–August, up 86% year on year, before the subsequent recovery in shipments. Panamax vessels account for the largest share of the displayed grain movements, with the US Gulf remaining the principal loading region alongside Pacific coast exports. COAL | POLICY AND QUOTAS RESHAPE ASIAN SUPPLY China is balancing tighter mine-safety oversight with efforts to maintain domestic coal supply ahead of the winter heating season. September raw coal output fell 6.8% y/y to 385 Mt, a decline attributed in reporting to stricter safety inspections after the May accident in Shanxi and a fatal accident in Hunan in August. On 16 October, the NDRC and the National Energy Administration urged Shanxi to bring idled mines back into operation and raise output before winter. India continues to prioritise domestic coal production and rail distribution to power plants. The Ministry of Coal reported average daily supply to the power sector rising from 2.2 Mt in September to 2.5 Mt over 1–10 October, with rail loading up from 426 to 469 rakes per day. The Power Secretary ruled out a mandatory imported-coal blending requirement for power plants this year. Indonesia 2027 coal production quotas under review: Indonesia opened applications for its 2027 production plans (RKAB) on 1 October, with submissions due by 15 November. The government is assessing production allocations, while uncertainty over approved volumes has already slowed negotiations for 2027 coal supply contracts. For the dry bulk freight market, the outcome will be important for Indonesian export commitments and prospective coal cargo availability across Asian routes. IRON ORE AND GRAIN | SUPPLY RISKS Iron ore – Saldanha terminal reaches scheduled maintenance deadline. South Africa’s Saldanha Iron Ore Terminal is scheduled to complete its 16-day maintenance programme on 21 October, following repairs to shiploaders, conveyors and rail tipplers. Separately, maintenance on the Sishen–Saldanha railway was scheduled to conclude on 16 October. With the terminal handling more than 50 million tonnes of iron ore annually, Capesize employment will focus on resuming loading operations and timing export cargoes after the shutdown. Transnet’s longer-term investment in rail and terminal infrastructure aims to improve the reliability of South Africa’s iron ore export corridor. Grain – wheat supply shifts and stronger U.S. corn export prospects. USDA’s October outlook points to tighter global wheat trade and stronger U.S. corn export prospects for 2026/27. Reduced wheat export availability from Russia and the United States, partly offset by Argentina and Canada, places greater importance on where importers secure their cargoes. Black Sea disruptions add pressure to sourcing decisions, particularly for buyers in North Africa and Asia. Grain – Black Sea attacks intensify pressure on Ukraine’s export corridors. Maritime security risks escalated in mid-October after HS Dignity sank and Chelsea 3 was damaged in reported drone attacks off Bulgaria on 13 October. Russia subsequently claimed strikes on Ukraine’s Izmail port and commercial vessels on 15 October, although these claims remain independently unverified. Ukraine’s grain and pulse exports reached 5.44 million tonnes by 7 October, down 24% year on year, with wheat shipments falling 42%. Worsening Black Sea security has increased reliance on alternative export corridors, particularly the Danube route through Izmail, Reni and Romania’s Constanța, while Baltic ports are also being explored. Congestion at the Sulina Canal has added to the pressure, with vessel waiting times previously exceeding two weeks. The European Council called on 16 October for the restoration of safe commercial navigation and further support for the EU–Ukraine Solidarity Lanes. For Handysize and smaller bulk carriers, the shift towards alternative loading ports, longer waiting times and higher freight costs is changing voyage economics, although additional corridor capacity remains constrained by security risks and inland logistics bottlenecks. OIL | CRUDE FLOWS IN FOCUS Crude Trade Geography: Shifting Origin and Loading-Port Shares Geopolitical disruptions are reshaping the geography of seaborne crude trade, with changes in supply origins, loading terminals and destination markets becoming more pronounced in 2026. Signal Ocean data highlights a greater share of crude originating from Russia, the UAE and the United States, alongside a shift in loading activity towards Fujairah and away from Ras Tanura and Basrah. On the demand side, India’s share has increased while China’s has declined. 2025 – Saudi Arabia held the largest share of seaborne crude origins at 13.6%, ahead of Russia (10.9%) and the United States (8.3%). China accounted for 22.9% of destinations, more than twice India’s 10.6% share. At the loading-port level, Ras Tanura led with 11.3%, reflecting the importance of Saudi export infrastructure in the distribution of crude cargoes. 2026 – A different supply ranking and a shift in loading geography. Russia (12.3%) and the UAE (11.0%) have moved ahead of Saudi Arabia (10.3%) in the January–September origin distribution, while Iraq’s share has fallen from 7.5% to 3.6%. The most pronounced change is at the loading-port level: Fujairah’s share has risen from 2.8% to 9.2%, overtaking Ras Tanura, whose share has declined from 11.3% to 4.0%. This redistribution is particularly relevant for tanker deployment, as greater loading activity outside the Strait of Hormuz changes where vessels need to position for their next cargo. On the destination side, China remains the largest market, although its share has declined from 22.9% to 17.6%, while India’s has increased from 10.6% to 11.8%. OIL | REGULATORY ENVIRONMENT Crude and fleet Graham Act waiver. The 16 October US executive order implementing the Graham Act waived specified new sanctions and duties, including the additional 100% duty on new purchases of Russian-origin crude oil and natural gas by the five largest importers from 18 October. The waivers remain in effect until the President or the Secretary of State decides further action is appropriate; sanctions under earlier executive orders remain in force. Sanctioned-tanker sales – under consideration. US officials have outlined a possible route for legitimate buyers to acquire sanctioned tankers, subject to OFAC authorisation and removal of vessel sanctions on a case-by-case basis, for employment in non-sanctioned trades.OFAC’s public notices reviewed through 20 October did not identify a general authorisation or vessel delistings implementing the initiative. The implications for tanker supply depend on how many vessels secure approval and return to commercial service, and when. Until those steps are confirmed, the initiative cannot be treated as an increase in available tonnage or evidence of freight relief. Oil products Russian diesel exports resume, with first US-bound shipment scheduled. The US licence issued on 9 October, alongside Russia’s partial easing of its diesel export ban from 10 October, has opened the way for additional Russian diesel shipments. The first confirmed export movement involved approximately 40,000 tonnes of ultra-low sulphur diesel loaded at Primorsk on 13 October, bound for Morocco. On 21 October, Russia announced plans to dispatch its first US-bound diesel cargo of 40,000 tonnes on 22 October, with further shipments expected. The US exemption covers specified Russian-origin diesel transactions until 7 April 2027, but does not extend to crude oil. For product tankers, the resumption introduces additional cargo opportunities from Russian export terminals, with the destination mix and pace of subsequent loadings determining the impact on vessel employment and tonne-mile demand. India – lower diesel export duty improves shipment economics. Effective 16 October, India reduced the special additional excise duty on diesel exports from INR 16 to INR 8.5 per litre, while increasing the petrol export duty from INR 0.5 to INR 2.5 per litre. The jet-fuel duty remained unchanged at INR 10.5 per litre. The reduction lowers the tax burden on diesel exports and could encourage additional overseas sales, subject to refinery output, domestic requirements and international demand. China – October fuel export approvals support renewed shipments. Beijing reportedly approved approximately 3.7 million tonnes of diesel, gasoline and jet-fuel exports for October following the Golden Week holiday. These approvals provide scope for Chinese refiners to resume overseas sales, although the volume represents reported export authorisations rather than confirmed shipments. The pace of cargo nominations and loading activity will determine the additional product tanker demand. IEA – Diesel stock releases add to available supply. On 15 October, the International Energy Agency outlined plans to accelerate the release of remaining emergency stocks, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel. The additional supply could help meet immediate product requirements, although the impact on seaborne trade will depend on where inventories are released and whether buyers source replacement cargoes internationally. Easing export restrictions in Russia, lower diesel export duties in India and new Chinese export approvals improve the outlook for clean petroleum product shipments. IEA stock releases, however, may limit immediate import demand in receiving markets. OIL | DISRUPTIONS AND RECOVERY Crude US Gulf – Offshore production recovery supports export availability. US offshore oil shut-ins declined from 1.46 million b/d on 9 October to 329,059 b/d on 13 October, equivalent to 16.1% of Gulf production. By 14 October, approximately 202,000 b/d (9.9%) remained offline. EIA data released on 15 October showed US commercial crude inventories falling by 8.6 million barrels in the week ended 9 October. The restoration of offshore output improves the supply outlook for US Gulf crude exports, although additional tanker demand will depend on refinery requirements, export nominations and confirmed loadings. Saudi Arabia – Houthi attack raises security concerns at Shaybah oilfield. On 21 October, Saudi authorities reported intercepting a drone targeting Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield. Falling debris reportedly caused a fire outside the processing facility, killing two workers, but oilfield operations were not disrupted. The incident adds to security concerns surrounding Saudi energy infrastructure without establishing a reduction in crude production or exports. Oil products Ryazan refinery – Partial processing disruption following drone attack. The 15 October attack forced the shutdown of Ryazan’s CDU-6 crude distillation unit, with an estimated processing capacity of 160,000 b/d, accounting for almost half the refinery’s total capacity. Three other crude distillation units remained operational, limiting the extent of the disruption. No confirmed restart of CDU-6 has been reported, while the impact on diesel production and export volumes remains unquantified. Petersburg Oil Terminal. Fire raises uncertainty over Baltic product shipments. A drone attack overnight on 18 October caused a fire at Petersburg Oil Terminal, a Baltic export facility handling gasoil, jet fuel, fuel oil and vacuum gasoil. The city governor confirmed the fire, while the extent of damage to loading infrastructure and any interruption to export operations remains unclear. No confirmed cargo cancellations or quantified export losses have been established. Any restrictions on terminal operations could delay product loadings and affect vessel turnaround times, with the freight impact dependent on the duration of the disruption and subsequent cargo schedules. US Gulf production recovery improves crude availability, while attacks on Russian energy infrastructure raise uncertainty over Baltic product shipments despite the easing of diesel export restrictions. KEY TAKEAWAY Recent developments highlight how freight conditions can tighten without a corresponding increase in cargo volumes. Disruptions to loading schedules, port operations and export programmes can delay vessel turnaround and temporarily reduce available tonnage. In a market where cargo flows and vessel positioning are changing rapidly, operational efficiency is becoming an important factor in short-term freight performance, alongside underlying supply-demand fundamentals. Meanwhile, oil cargo flows may be shaped by shifting product-export rules and updated sanctions policies, alongside loading schedule risks driven by refinery outages and the Petersburg terminal fire.
