articles.title: The Week in Alt Fuels: The methanol bunker footprint
articles.summary: Methanol bunkering has spread across Europe, Asia and parts of North America, with more ports, physical suppliers and bunker vessels coming into the picture. Several methanol bunker locations have been established in Europe. TankMatch and UniBarge are among the physical suppliers supporting deliveries in the...
articles.body: The Week in Alt Fuels: The methanol bunker footprint in International Shipping News 24/10/2026 Methanol bunkering has spread across Europe, Asia and parts of North America, with more ports, physical suppliers and bunker vessels coming into the picture. Several methanol bunker locations have been established in Europe. TankMatch and UniBarge are among the physical suppliers supporting deliveries in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) region. Methanol bunker operations have been reported at Gothenburg, Hamburg and Immingham. Bremerhaven and Kiel have demonstrated varying levels of readiness through early operations and trials. Some suppliers like Repsol and Mureloil are ready to offer physical methanol deliveries at Spanish ports, including Bilbao, Mugardos and Barcelona. A particularly broad network of ports has developed across Asia, with methanol bunker operations becoming more common. Several ports across China have hosted methanol bunkering, including Shanghai, Ningbo-Zhoushan, Guangzhou, Qingdao, Dalian and Shenzhen. Suppliers including CIMC Enric, SIPG Energy and China Marine Bunker offer ship-to-ship deliveries across Chinese ports. Activity has also extended to Hong Kong, where Sinopec and Chimbusco Pan Nation have supplied bio-methanol. Elsewhere in Asia, methanol bunkering has been conducted at Busan and Ulsan in South Korea, and Japanese ports including Yokohama and Kinoe. The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) has issued five-year methanol bunker licences to PetroChina, Golden Island and Global Energy Trading that have been effective since January. But the MPA reported no methanol bunker sales in September, extending the streak to seven consecutive months. The Port of Houston in the US hosted a ship-to-ship methanol bunker operation in March, with 2,000 mt of methanol delivered to Tangier Maersk. This was preceded by a barge-to-ship operation in April 2023, when the tankers Stena Pro Marine and Stena Prosperous, owned by the Proman Stena Bulk joint venture, took a total of 2,600 mt of methanol from a Kirby barge. The vessels behind the deliveries The number of bunker barges and chemical tankers capable of carrying methanol and offering ship-to-ship bunkering at these ports has also grown steadily over the years. Golden Centaurus, Golden Antares, Golden Sirius, Anna Cosulich and Vanda Pioneer are among the vessels capable of carrying out methanol bunker deliveries in Singapore. China’s supply network includes Daqing 268, Zhongran Green Energy 85and Jia Chen 17, serving different parts of the country’s coastal bunker market. European operations have involved Evidence and Chicago around the ARA region, Odyssee in northwestern Europe, Bahía Candela in Spain and Nore around Gothenburg and Skaw. Japan’s Eika Maru has supported methanol bunkering at Yokohama. In the US, the barge Kirby 29067 has delivered methanol to Tangier Maersk. Many of these vessels also supply biofuels or conventional bunkers, so being able to deliver methanol does not mean they are always available to do so. The next wave of ports Many other ports are preparing for future methanol demand. VO Chidambaranar, Mumbai and Kandla in India, Seattle, Tacoma, Long Beach and South Louisiana in the US, and Auckland in New Zealand are among the ports exploring or developing methanol bunker capabilities over the next couple of years, although their levels of progress vary considerably. Port authorities in Dhofar in Oman, and Algeciras and Valencia in Spain, have also discussed developing methanol bunker capabilities, but have yet to announce timelines. The overall geographical spread shows that methanol bunkering is moving towards a broader network of potential supply locations. The next challenge is turning that geographical reach into dependable availability, so that ships can obtain methanol not simply where it has been bunkered before, but where and when they actually need it. In other alt fuels news this week, the Zero Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance (ZEMBA) has delivered 82,000 mtCO2-equivalent (mtCO2e) in emissions reductions in 2025 and 2026 under its first low-emission shipping tender with Hapag-Lloyd, which concluded this month. South Korean shipping firm HMM has ordered eight 13,000 TEU LNG-capable container ships from HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and HD Hyundai Samho for delivery from 2029. The vessels will be deployed on its Far East-India-Mediterranean service, HMM said. Danish operator Maersk Tankers plans to retrofit up to 10 very large ammonia carriers (VLACs) with ammonia dual-fuel engines, but said the final decision will “depend on securing commercial commitments from customers”. Source: By Konica Bhatt, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news/ 2026-10-24 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: GMS Week 43 – Freight Refuses to Stay Down
articles.summary: Last week’s dry freight retreat appeared to offer recycling buyers the opening they had been waiting for. It did not last. articles.body: GMS Week 43 – Freight Refuses to Stay Down in Weekly Demolition Reports 24/10/2026 Last week’s dry freight retreat appeared to offer recycling buyers the opening they had been waiting for. It did not last. The Baltic Dry Index recovered from 2,545 on October 15 to 2,693 on Thursday, October 22, led by improving Capesize earnings. Although still below earlier October levels, the recovery has restored some confidence in continued trading. For recyclers hoping that softer freight would finally release ageing bulkers, the window of opportunity has already narrowed. The energy market supplied a more worrying development. Renewed Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia heightened concerns over Middle Eastern oil supplies, prompting Saudi Aramco to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters on Thursday. Brent climbed above USD 115 per barrel intraday on Friday, its highest level since early May, while WTI moved above USD 100. With Gulf shipping risks and elevated insurance costs continuing to disrupt normal trading patterns, ageing tankers still have compelling reasons to remain employed rather than head for recycling. Dry bulk’s recovery was uneven. Capesizes strengthened to 3,848, while Supramaxes advanced to 1,890. Panamaxes, however, retreated to 2,151, illustrating the different pressures facing individual vessel segments. The broader message remains unchanged: freight earnings and second-hand alternatives continue to discourage owners from releasing sufficient recycling candidates. One week’s decline was encouraging. Its partial reversal has reminded buyers how quickly that encouragement can disappear. Steel markets offered little common direction. Indian plate strengthened during the week, while Bangladesh, Pakistan and China remained unchanged. Domestic finished-steel consumption continues to disappoint across much of the sub-continent, limiting the benefit of otherwise stable steel quotations. Turkey weakened marginally against the international market, although its central bank reduced interest rates from 37% to 36%, offering modest financing relief amid continued currency pressure. Physical waterfront activity nevertheless continued. Alang received additional general cargo and reefer tonnage, Chattogram completed several smaller vessel deliveries, and Gadani welcomed another previously secured bulker. These movements sustain yard operations without signalling a corresponding improvement in fresh recycling sales. The distinction remains important: ships are reaching the beaches, but the next pipeline is still far from full. Bangladesh continues to display the strongest conventional buying appetite, although suitable candidates remain scarce. Pakistan retains healthy underlying demand with greater purchasing discipline, while India continues to benefit from specialist opportunities and improving local steel. Turkey remains cautious as weak domestic consumption restricts further buying enthusiasm. The final quarter is therefore developing much as it began, with buyers seeking tonnage that owners have little urgency to release. Freight has recovered, steel offers mixed support, and recycling demand remains largely intact. The beaches are ready for more business. The ships, for now, still have other plans. articles.title: Seafarers face widening competency gap as digital shipping accelerates, recent research finds
articles.summary: Eighty two per cent of maritime professionals surveyed say current training does not adequately prepare crews for the realities of modern, digitally-enabled vessel operations. Just 18% believe training keeps pace, according to new research from OneOcean and Thetius. Seafarer training is falling behind rapidly...
articles.body: Seafarers face widening competency gap as digital shipping accelerates, recent research finds in International Shipping News 24/10/2026 Eighty two per cent of maritime professionals surveyed say current training does not adequately prepare crews for the realities of modern, digitally-enabled vessel operations. Just 18% believe training keeps pace, according to new research from OneOcean and Thetius. Seafarer training is falling behind rapidly evolving operational realities at sea, according to two new reports commissioned by OneOcean and conducted by maritime innovation consultancy Thetius. The research draws on survey data and interviews with maritime professionals across shipboard and shore-based roles. Those interviewed and surveyed include masters, officers, engineers, superintendents, training personnel, crewing staff, and shore-based operators. Findings reveal two interconnected challenges – that seafarers work in increasingly complex digital environments, and that maritime professionals do not feel well prepared to keep pace with this change. The reports suggest that whilst the global seafaring workforce may be qualified on paper, it is under prepared in practice. According to the first report, Competent or Compliant?, the research found that: 82% of respondents say current training models do not prepare crews for modern operations 52% report that qualified crew struggle in real operations ‘often’ or ‘very often’ 56% say ‘tick box’ compliance contributes to this gap 18% believe current training adequately prepares crews for operational reality The maritime professionals that responded say these competence ‘gaps’ are most visible during: Abnormal or unexpected situations (67%) High-pressure operations (56%) Working between different vessels (36%) When using complex digital systems, ECDIS or reporting tools (31%) According to the second report, Decision-optimised or overloaded? the digital revolution has introduced novel risks alongside new capabilities because the technology can redistribute rather than eliminate work. Modern vessels are highly connected digital ecosystems, and while this has improved reporting, transparency and efficiency, it has also had introduced challenges. Crews increasingly act as the link between systems that do not communicate with one another, manually reconciling conflicting data across displays. The report also found that alert fatigue is a growing risk. For example, following Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) interference, 75% of mariners reported a moderate to significant increase in workload, showing how quickly information overload can escalate when further systems alarm at once. The report suggests that more data does not necessarily lead to better decisions, particularly in high-pressure situations, yet training courses do not sufficiently prepare seafarers to handle this reality. Alex Mangan, Chief Marketing and Communications Officer, OneOcean, said: “Change in shipping will only accelerate as vessels adopt new digital systems to manage tightening international regulation and to sail more efficiently and productively. “This has created a growing gap between the training seafarers receive and the challenges they face at sea. The problem is twofold, coming from rapid technological changes at sea, and from the ways in which training is delivered to crews. Closing this reality gap requires the industry to shift its approaches to competence, to reflect real-world operations.” Nick Chubb, Founder of Thetius, said: “The findings reveal a clear reality gap between the demands of modern shipping and the way competence is developed. As vessels become more digitally complex, the industry must move beyond compliance-based training and equip seafarers with the skills they need to operate safely and effectively.” OneOcean’s own product suite reflects this thinking. The Ocean Learning Platform (OLP) gives operators fleet-wide visibility into crew readiness, turning certification records and assessments into a verified picture of who’s ready, where training gaps remain and, crucially, painting a clear picture of competence levels. OneOcean remains committed to investing in Human Capital Management and empowering continuous workforce planning, development and engagement through digital tools. Both reports were launched via a two-part webinar series hosted by Thetius, featuring live discussion of the findings with industry panellists. The reports and the webinar recordings are available at https://www.oneocean.com/insights/oneocean-thetius-thought-leadership . OneOcean continued the conversation this week at Seatrade Maritime Crew Connect Global’s where Capt. Sanjeev Mathur, SVP, OneOcean, moderated a peer exchange focussed on ‘The Deployment Gap: What the Officer Shortage Actually Costs to Manage’, John Butler, SVP, Technical Ship Management, OneOcean, discussed ‘The Fatigue Timebomb & Shore Leave Erosion: A Witness Stand’ and Anna Ruszczynska – Regional Director – APAC, OneOcean, debated ‘The 800,000 — Who Owns the Race to Train the Guinea Pig Generation?’. Source: OneOcean 2026-10-24 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Rotterdam’s conventional bunker sales rebound 10% from previous quarter in Port News 24/10/2026 Changes between the second quarter and the third quarter of 2026: • HSFO sales up by 50,000 mt to 755,000 mt • VLSFO sales up by 73,000 mt to 427,000 mt • MGO sales up by 18,000 mt to 349,000 mt • ULSFO sales up by 42,000 mt to 165,000 mt • LNG sales down by 26,000 mt to 97,000 mt • No grey methanol sales Bunker suppliers in Rotterdam sold 1.8 million mt of conventional marine fuels in the third quarter of this year, up 10% from the second quarter, according to data from Port of Rotterdam. Volumes in the second quarter of this year had fallen to their lowest level since the port’s records began in 2010. Conventional fuels sales’ share as a percentage of the port’s total bunker sales rose to 92% in the third quarter, from 87% in the second quarter. Fuel oil grades lead recovery HSFO remained Rotterdam’s best-selling conventional fuel grade, accounting for 42% of conventional bunker sales, and 39% of total sales. HSFO sales rose 7% from the previous quarter to 755,000 mt. VLSFO sales jumped 21% from the previous quarter to 427,000 mt, the grade’s steepest quarterly gain since 2021. VLSFO accounted for 24% of conventional bunker sales. ULSFO sales surged 34% from the previous quarter to 165,000 mt, also its steepest quarterly gain since 2021. The grade made up 9% of conventional fuel sales. MGO sales rose 5% from the previous quarter to 349,000 mt, accounting for 19% of conventional fuel sales. Nine-month sales well below last year Rotterdam’s conventional bunker sales fell 26% year-on-year to 5.1 million mt in the first nine months of 2026, from 6.9 million mt in the same period last year. VLSFO sales dropped the most, falling 42% to 1.2 million mt. HSFO sales declined 21% to 2.1 million mt. LNG bucking the trend LNG bunker sales fell 21% from the previous quarter to 97,000 mt. LNG’s share of Rotterdam’s total bunker sales slipped to 5%, from 7% in the second quarter. LNG sales dropped 35% in the third quarter, compared to the same quarter last year. Rotterdam recorded 324,000 mt of LNG sales in the first three quarters, down 10% compared to the same period last year. Photo courtesy Philly Shipyard By Ira Breskin BRONX, NY — Vessel Construction Management practices received praise at the Shipbuilding in America conference here this week. Vessel Construction Management (VCM) essentially outsources oversight of a ship’s entire construction process, from design to delivery, to a third party acting as the owner’s representative. The vessel construction manager takes charge of the entire project, from procuring materials to testing the vessel before delivery. The Maritime Administration (MARAD) recently embraced VCM when procuring a new generation of training ships for five of the six state maritime academies. To date, MARAD contractor TOTE Services has delivered four of the five vessels. “The goal is to deliver a newbuild ship on time and on budget by reducing direct government involvement with the yard and making the construction process more commercial than normal government procurement,” said Charlie Papavizas, an attorney with Winston Taylor in Washington, D.C. The next challenge is to expand the use of VCM in commercial shipbuilding, said Chris Clark, vice president of new construction at TOTE Services, during the conference. The conference was held earlier this week at the State University of New York Maritime College. Empire State VII, the school’s new training ship, was the first in the series to be delivered on time and within budget by TOTE, arriving in September 2023. TOTE Services is also using VCM practices in two subsequent government projects: the construction of missile range instrumentation vessels and a new class of medium landing ships for the Navy. Several ship operators and ship management companies offer VCM services, with the scope of those services depending on each firm’s expertise. VCM relies on commercial shipbuilding best practices and commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) components rather than military-specification parts, both of which can reduce vessel costs and speed delivery. Moreover, the use of VCM minimizes unnecessary design changes and the resulting change orders, which are often a source of costly contract disputes. articles.title: China Militia Boats Expand 'Battlefield Prep', says Taiwan
articles.summary: China is combining militia vessels with coast guard ships to expand "battlefield preparation" around Taiwan and into the western Pacific, Taiwan's Coast Guard said, warning the operations were also putting pressure on Japan and the Philippines.Responding…
articles.body: China Militia Boats Expand 'Battlefield Prep', says Taiwan Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Copyright TomKorcak/AdobeStock China is combining militia vessels with coast guard ships to expand "battlefield preparation" around Taiwan and into the western Pacific, Taiwan's Coast Guard said, warning the operations were also putting pressure on Japan and the Philippines. Responding to a Reuters exclusive this month on the first known sighting of a Chinese militia boat off Taiwan's Pacific coast in mid-August, the coast guard said it had dispatched a patrol boat to drive away the vessel, which was operating alongside a Chinese coast guard ship and a research vessel. The coast guard confirmed details in the Reuters report, identifying the suspected militia fishing boat as Minfudingyu 07902 , and said it had come as close as about 2.7 nautical miles outside Taiwan's restricted waters on August 16. China has increased such activity since June in overlapping economic waters involving Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, the coast guard said, after Tokyo and Manila announced talks on maritime boundary delimitation in their exclusive economic zones. EEZs extend 200 nautical miles from the coast and give a coastal state rights to exploit, conserve and manage natural resources in those waters. "Such complex grey-zone operations not only increase the maritime surveillance and response burden on Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, but may also create regional security pressure and affect the existing international maritime order," Taiwan's Coast Guard said in a statement to Reuters. China's defence ministry, and the Philippines defence and foreign ministries did not immediately respond to requests for comment.Japan's coast guard declined immediate comment. The coast guard said the vessels' coordinated activity was part of a broader pattern of Chinese "grey-zone" operations using law-enforcement, scientific and civilian cover to expand Beijing's influence at sea while remaining below the threshold of open conflict. The Chinese operations were aimed at "assisting 'battlefield preparation'," the coast guard said, adding Taiwan's east coast was an important maritime traffic and supply route and that continued Chinese activity there could further increase security pressure on Taiwan. Officials in Taiwan say they believe China is practicing for a possible maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets. China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has not ruled out the use of force to achieve its goals. Taiwan's government rejects the claim and says only the island's people can decide their future. China has repeatedly said its operations off Taiwan's east coast are "legitimate and lawful" because they are in Chinese waters, a position Taipei's government strongly rejects. Taiwan's coast guard said it had placed the Minfudingyu 07902 on a priority watchlist, assessing the boat showed the "characteristics" of Chinese maritime militia activity and said it would continue tracking the vessel. Dating back to the 1950s, China's maritime militia uses fishing vessels with trained, state-supported crews to operate in disputed waters, often alongside coast guard ships around South China Sea flashpoints, helping Beijing assert maritime claims while maintaining a civilian appearance. The surveillance report reviewed by Reuters was conducted by Taiwan's Apex Aviation, which used radar screenshots, infrared imagery and automatic-identification system data from a reconnaissance flight to document the cluster of vessels. (Reuters)

REUTERS/Carlos Barria/File Photo The Trump administration is proposing to extend its suspension of port fees targeting China-linked vessels for another two months, pushing their potential return into January 2027 as Washington and Beijing continue negotiations over China’s dominance of global shipbuilding. The proposal, outlined in a Federal Register notice scheduled for publication October 26, would extend the existing one-year suspension through January 9, 2027. The current pause is set to expire November 9. The extension would provide another reprieve for shipping companies facing potentially significant fees on Chinese-owned, Chinese-operated and Chinese-built vessels calling at U.S. ports, as well as certain foreign-built vehicle carriers. “The United States is continuing to engage with China with the goal of obtaining the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices at issue in the investigation,” USTR said in the notice. Under the proposal, the measures would remain suspended from November 10, 2026, through January 9, 2027. During that period, shipping companies would not incur liability for port fees under Annexes I, II and III of the original Section 301 action. The suspension would also continue to cover certain duties on ship-to-shore cranes and cargo-handling equipment. The proposed extension comes nearly a year after President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to suspend the port fees as part of a broader trade agreement reached in South Korea. Washington began collecting the fees on October 14, 2025, but suspended them on November 10, meaning the measures were in effect for less than four weeks. China also suspended its retaliatory fees on U.S.-linked vessels. The original measures emerged from a Section 301 investigation launched during the Biden administration following a 2024 petition by the United Steelworkers and other labor organizations. The investigation concluded that China’s industrial policies and subsidies distorted global competition and undermined U.S. commerce. The resulting port fees became a central part of the Trump administration’s strategy to counter China’s maritime dominance and encourage investment in American shipbuilding. Growing Pressure to Reinstate Fees The latest proposal comes despite mounting pressure from some lawmakers and maritime labor groups to bring the fees back. In June, Senators Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) urged the administration to immediately reinstate the measures , arguing that their suspension undermined efforts to rebuild the U.S. commercial shipbuilding industry. “Section 301 port fees are critical to revitalizing U.S. shipbuilding,” the senators wrote in a letter to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The lawmakers pointed to China’s growing share of global shipbuilding, noting that Chinese yards now account for more than half of global commercial vessel production, compared with just 0.1% for the United States. They also questioned whether Washington had secured meaningful concessions from Beijing in exchange for suspending the fees and how the administration intended to fund its proposed Maritime Security Trust Fund without the revenue. Maritime labor unions have similarly criticized the suspension, arguing that it weakens one of the few measures specifically designed to counter China’s state-supported shipbuilding industry. Shipping companies, meanwhile, have welcomed the reprieve. The original fees threatened to impose substantial costs on carriers and disrupt established shipping networks. During the brief period the measures were active, U.S. carrier Matson reported incurring $6.4 million in reciprocal Chinese port fees, while China’s state-owned COSCO faced an estimated $1.5 billion in annual U.S. charges. Andy Abbott, CEO of ACL, told gCaptain that any port fees would impact its growing US export business, and customers are concerned ACL. “ACL’s unique ships were mistakenly classified by USTR as vehicle carriers even though only 1% of its cargo is automobiles,” explained Abbott. “Our largest US container and heavy machinery customers were panicking that we would redeploy our ships out of the US trade to the booming China trade. This development allows us to continue serving the US market with the fastest transit times from the US East Coast to Europe.” The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) and World Shipping Council both welcomed last year’s suspension, warning that the competing U.S. and Chinese measures risked increasing transportation costs and disrupting global trade. A Broader Debate Over Port Fees The proposed extension also comes as the administration considers a much broader port fee system under its Maritime Action Plan , unveiled earlier this year. Unlike the China-specific Section 301 measures, the plan envisions fees on all foreign-built commercial vessels calling at U.S. ports, with proceeds supporting domestic shipbuilding through a proposed Maritime Security Trust Fund. The plan outlined potential fees ranging from 1 cent to 25 cents per kilogram of imported cargo, which the administration estimated could generate as much as $1.5 trillion over 10 years at the upper end. ICS has warned that such broad-based charges could significantly increase shipping costs and disrupt global trade, even as it supports efforts to expand U.S. shipbuilding capacity. The proposals underscore the competing pressures facing the administration as it seeks to revive American shipyards without imposing additional costs on U.S. importers, exporters and consumers. For now, the latest USTR proposal would leave the China-specific port fee measures on hold for another two months, while negotiations continue. USTR has opened a public comment period on the extension, with submissions due by 5 p.m. Eastern Time on October 30. Comments can be filed through the USTR public comment portal under docket USTR-2026-0694. The extension has not yet been finalized. The notice also does not address whether China will extend its own suspension of retaliatory fees on U.S.-linked vessels. articles.title: Record Tanker Rates Threaten to Push U.S. Oil Exports to Asia to Seven-Year Low
articles.summary: US crude oil exports to Asia are set to hit multi-year lows after the Iran war disrupted global shipping and pushed the cost to lease a tanker for the Pacific journey to a record of almost $80 million.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche By Yongchang Chin and Nathan Risser (Bloomberg) –US crude oil exports to Asia are set to hit multi-year lows after the Iran war disrupted global shipping and pushed the cost to lease a tanker for the Pacific journey to a record of almost $80 million. Asian refinery orders for US crude for delivery in November tumbled roughly 50% to 24 million to 26 million barrels this month sequentially, according to traders who asked for anonymity because they weren’t authorized to publicly comment. If that pace of orders holds through the end of this month, it would mark a seven-year low, based on ship-tracking data from Kpler and Vortexa. The tanker rate along the US Gulf Coast-to-China route has more than tripled since the US-Iran conflict erupted in late February to almost $60 million as of Thursday, according to Baltic Exchange figures. Earlier in the month, it touched $79.6 million, an unprecedented ruction in a market where rates averaged less than $8 million in the half decade before the conflict. As it stands, leasing the largest class of crude carriers for the 30-day voyage is equivalent to half the cost of building a brand-new vessel. Those eye-watering rates doesn’t include the cost of the oil itself, which is trading around $100 a barrel. Cost to Ship US Oil to Asia Has Never Been Higher “The main story right now in the market is freight rates,” Randy Hawkins, Valero Energy Inc.’s head of oil trading, said during as conference call with analysts. Tanker rates are so inflated that refiners are effectively spending $30 to $35 to haul each barrel of crude from the Gulf Coast to Asia, or as much as seven times what they shelled out last year, Hawkins said. IEA: Gulf Oil Shipping Costs Top $37 Per Barrel, Five Times Pre-War Levels To be sure, the end of the November trading cycle isn’t a hard deadline, which leaves some leeway for traders to snap up last-minutes cargoes. At least one market participant who asked to remain anonymous said Asia-bound US cargoes for November may recover to as much as 40 million barrels in post-cycle trades. Vortexa, however, is skeptical that such a turnaround is imminent. “We don’t currently see evidence of a near-term surge that would push those volumes significantly higher,” said Rohit Rathod, a senior Vortexa analyst. The drop in Asian demand appears to be rippling across US crude pricing. Export-bound Permian Basin oil was trading for 25 cents above the benchmark futures contract at the Magellan East Houston hub as of Wednesday, down from more than $3 six weeks earlier, according to Link Data Services. Medium sour export grade Mars, which is pumped from deepwater wells in the Gulf of Mexico and is similar to Middle Eastern crude, has seen its premium to futures plunge to $6 from $17.50 in late March. US Oil Exports Surged to Record High This Year | The US sent over 6 million barrels of oil abroad each day in late April as war curtailed flows from the Middle East Valero’s Hawkins said one factor hindering global tanker availability has been the increased use of smaller vessels to pick up crude in the Persian Gulf that are less likely to be hit by Iranian fire in Strait of Hormuz. Once they’ve traversed the waterway, their cargoes are transferred to larger vessels waiting in the Gulf of Oman. “The inefficient process of this ship-to-ship transferring that they’re doing of crude oil in the Gulf of Oman is really tying up global shipping and to require more tankers to move the same amount of oil,” Hawkins said. Insurance rates and high fuel costs also are driving up freight costs, he added. “The primary factor remains high freight costs, which continue to squeeze arbitrage economics for long-haul routes,” Vortexa’s Rathod said. “The incentive for Asian buyers to source from the US Gulf Coast has diminished.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Brent Crude Prices Reach Five-Month High Amidst Continued Houthi Attacks, UAE Oil Spill
articles.summary: Oil prices rose on Friday, with Brent crude touching its highest since early May, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East where UAE authorities also reported an oil spill.Brent crude futures gained $1.71…
articles.body: Brent Crude Prices Reach Five-Month High Amidst Continued Houthi Attacks, UAE Oil Spill Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Аня Крамарова Oil prices rose on Friday, with Brent crude touching its highest since early May, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East where UAE authorities also reported an oil spill . Brent crude futures gained $1.71, or 1.5%, to $114.99 a barrel by 1300 GMT, having earlier reached $115.16, the highest level since May 4. US West Texas Intermediate crude gained $1.80, or 1.8%, to $101.27. The Brent benchmark is on track for a 4.4% weekly rise, its third in a row, while WTI is poised to finish 0.4% down on the week. Saudi Aramco on Thursday ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported, as fighting intensified between the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen-based Houthis. An oil spill from a tanker was detected off the UAE coast of Umm Al Quwain, the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday. It did not say what caused the spill and authorities have not identified the tanker involved. Shipping sources said on October 9 that the Gem No.2 was struck by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera in the UAE. "The market remains concerned about a potential escalation, which, in a worst-case scenario, could trigger renewed supply disruptions," said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo, adding that volatile oil flows and elevated freight rates have left the market undersupplied. Clashes between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government have raged since the Iran-aligned Houthis pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb last month, a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea. In Libya, an oil pipeline valve from the Hamada and Tahara oilfields to Zawiya port has been shut, leading to a reduction in production at both fields, the head of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Thursday. Meanwhile, the first Russian diesel bound for the US since an export agreement between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday. Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of US midterm elections on November 3. (Reuters)

articles.title: Strait of Hormuz Ship Attacks Reach New High in October
articles.summary: October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017."October…
articles.body: Strait of Hormuz Ship Attacks Reach New High in October Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 © Adobe Stock/S.Gvozd October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017. "October has seen the highest number of ship attacks on record," said Noam Raydan, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. Raydan, who maintains the institute's interactive shipping incident map, has recorded 28 confirmed and reported attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways in October and 113 since the US-Israeli war with Iran began on February 28. The institute's map shows most of the attacks that took place in September and October were in the Strait of Hormuz. AROUND 3.5% OF WORLD SUPERTANKER FLEET ATTACKED The tally broadly aligns with data from the International Maritime Organization (IMO), which recorded a total of 120 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East since the conflict with Iran began. The IMO lists more than 30 supertankers, or Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs), that were damaged during the attacks, including 11 in October alone, a Reuters review of the IMO list and MarineTraffic vessel data showed. Each VLCC can carry about 2 million barrels of crude. The listed vessels account for about 3.5% of the total global VLCC fleet, which exceeds 900. More tankers came under attack as shipowners became increasingly willing to load cargoes inside the Gulf, lured by daily freight rates exceeding $1 million and steeper discounts offered by regional producers against dated Brent. "October 2026 has emerged as the most intense period of maritime attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the escalation of hostilities in March," Greece-based consultancy Marisks said. Between October 5 and October 11, a dozen ships were attacked, marking also the highest weekly number of attacks since the conflict began, it also said. NOT ALL ATTACKS MAY BE CAPTURED IN DATA By intensifying attacks, Iran is seeking to slow the recovery in shipments and maintain pressure on global energy markets ahead of November's US midterm elections, Raydan said. Earlier this month, Reuters reported about Tehran adopting such tactics, citing two senior Iranian officials. UKMTO, the British maritime security service, which recorded 135 incidents related to the US-Iran conflict as of October 16, said it was struggling to capture the whole picture due to insufficient voluntary reporting by shippers. The UKMTO data also showed a sharp rise in ship damage caused by attacks in October. articles.title: U.S. Navy Secretary Visits Fincantieri Wisconsin Shipyards
articles.summary: Fincantieri hosted Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao and senior federal officials at its Marinette and Sturgeon Bay shipyards in Wisconsin, highlighting investments in advanced manufacturing, automation and expanded shipbuilding capacity as the company prepares for construction of the U.S.
articles.body: U.S. Navy Secretary Visits Fincantieri Wisconsin Shipyards Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao visits Fincantieri shipyard in Wisconsin. Image courtesy Fincantieri Fincantieri hosted Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao and senior federal officials at its Marinette and Sturgeon Bay shipyards in Wisconsin, highlighting investments in advanced manufacturing, automation and expanded shipbuilding capacity as the company prepares for construction of the U.S. Navy's Landing Ship Medium (LSM) vessels . The delegation included Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, Maritime Administration Administrator Stephen Carmel, OMB Associate Director for Shipbuilding Jerry Hendrix and Eugenio Santagata , General Manager of Fincantieri's Naval Vessels Division. George Moutafis, CEO of Fincantieri Marine Group, and Jan Allman, CEO of Fincantieri Marinette Marine, outlined the company's shipbuilding programs, capital investments and efforts to accelerate production. At Marinette, officials toured the automated panel production line and observed demonstrations of collaborative robots, augmented and virtual reality tools, and powered air-purifying respirators. Fincantieri is integrating these technologies to improve production efficiency and worker safety. At Sturgeon Bay, the delegation reviewed the shipyard's capabilities and its role in supporting simultaneous construction of multiple vessel classes. "This vital federal investment allows us to modernize" is not part of this release; instead, Moutafis emphasized the company's investments in workforce capabilities and advanced technologies to increase production rates and meet Navy requirements. The visit comes as Fincantieri Marinette Marine prepares to begin construction of four LSM vessels for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, subject to negotiations with program manager TOTE Services. In April, the Navy awarded Fincantieri an initial $30 million contract for procurement of critical materials associated with the LSM program. "Our Navy needs more skilled professionals like those I had the opportunity to meet today in order to remain the strongest Navy in the world," Cao said. The Wisconsin facilities are positioned to serve as the industrial center for Fincantieri's LSM work, expanding their role in the U.S. naval shipbuilding industrial base. articles.body: 18th Tug Delivered by Sanmar Shipyards to SAAM Towage Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 © Sanmar Shipyards Sanmar Shipyards has delivered SAAM XIMBAL, a new BOGAÇAY Class tug, to SAAM Towage, marking the 18th SANMAR-built tug delivered to the towage operator since 2018. Known as BOGAÇAY XCVI during construction in Türkiye, SAAM XIMBAL will operate from the Port of Lázaro Cárdenas on Mexico's Pacific coast, supporting demanding ship-handling operations at one of the country's major commercial ports. SAAM XIMBAL is based on the RAmparts 2400SX-MK|I design, developed exclusively for SANMAR by Canadian naval architects Robert Allan Ltd. The latest delivery brings the number of BOGAÇAY Class tugs in the SAAM Towage fleet to 13. Powered by two CAT 3516E main engines, each producing 2,350 KW at 1,800 rpm, SAAM XIMBAL combines high performance with environmentally responsible operation. A high level of onboard automation supports operational efficiency, while a sewage treatment unit and oily water separator further reduce the vessel's environmental impact as per SAAM sustainability requisites With an overall length of 24.4 meters, a molded beam of 12 meters, a least moulded depth of 4.5 meters and a navigational draught of 5.45 meters, SAAM XIMBAL combines compact dimensions with the power required for demanding harbor operations. The tug delivers over 80 tonnes of bollard pull and achieves a free-running speed of 13 knots. It is also equipped with FiFi 1 firefighting capability, further enhancing its operational versatility. SAAM XIMBAL joins a diverse group of SANMAR-built vessels already operating in the SAAM Towage fleet. Alongside the 13 BOGAÇAY Class tugs, these include three all-electric ElectRA harbor tugs and two powerful BIGAÇAY Class RAstar 29005X tugs.

The FSO PTSC LDV is chartered to Murphy Cuu Long Bac Oil, a wholly owned subsidiary of Murphy Oil Corporation, under a ten-year firm contract with extension options of up to five additional years. October 23, 2026 Image courtesy Mammoet Image courtesy Mammoet Image courtesy Mammoet Image courtesy Mammoet Image courtesy Mammoet Mammoet Canada Eastern Ltd., Port of Argentia Inc. and Argentia Capital Inc. (ACI) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to advance plans for a floating dry dock and marine repair facility at the Port of Argentia in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada. The proposed development would combine Mammoet's heavy lifting, transport and marine engineering capabilities with the port's existing infrastructure, creating additional capacity for vessel maintenance, repair and industrial services. Central to the project is the Tugdock Submersible Platform (TSP) , developed by Mammoet subsidiary Tugdock Submersible Platforms Ltd. The modular floating dry dock system is designed to accommodate vessels of varying sizes and can be scaled to meet changing operational requirements, providing an alternative to conventional fixed dry dock infrastructure. "This partnership represents an exciting opportunity to build on Mammoet's established presence at Argentia and introduce advanced, scalable marine technology to the Canadian market," said Jeremy Asher, Managing Director at Mammoet. The partners envision a multi-client facility serving commercial shipping, offshore oil and gas, offshore wind, the Canadian Coast Guard and the Royal Canadian Navy. Mammoet already operates at Argentia, including work associated with the former Cenovus Graving Dock site and offshore wind marshalling projects. Scott Penney, CEO of Port of Argentia, said the agreement builds on the port's existing relationship with Mammoet and opportunities emerging across Canada's marine industry. The partners will next initiate a formal Expression of Interest process to identify an experienced international marine industrial operator capable of managing the proposed facility. The MOU represents an initial development step, with the partners seeking to establish a competitive marine repair operation while expanding Newfoundland and Labrador's industrial capacity and creating opportunities for regional suppliers and skilled trades.

articles.title: Rio Tinto targets larger capesizes in $1.9bn Australian bauxite push
articles.summary: Mining giant Rio Tinto has approved a $1.9bn investment in a major bauxite expansion in Australia’s Queensland state, including an upgrade of its export facilities to accommodate larger capesize bulk carriers. The Kangwinan project on the western Cape York Peninsula will add 20m tonnes of annual bauxite production...
articles.body: Dry Cargo Operations Rio Tinto targets larger capesizes in $1.9bn Australian bauxite push Adis Ajdin October 23, 2026 0 1,434 2 minutes read Bocimar Bocimar Mining giant Rio Tinto has approved a $1.9bn investment in a major bauxite expansion in Australia’s Queensland state, including an upgrade of its export facilities to accommodate larger capesize bulk carriers. The Kangwinan project on the western Cape York Peninsula will add 20m tonnes of annual bauxite production capacity, with first output targeted for 2029 and full production expected by 2032. The development will replace production from the ageing Andoom mine near Weipa, which is expected to reach the end of its life this decade, while also helping offset the planned closure of the Gove operation in the Northern Territory in 2029. Once fully operational, Kangwinan will lift annual capacity at Rio Tinto’s Weipa operations to around 44m tonnes, compared with current production of approximately 38m tonnes. The new mining centre will be located about 15 km southeast of Rio Tinto’s existing Amrun mine. A 15 km conveyor system will transport bauxite to expanded stockyards and the Amrun export wharf, which will be upgraded to handle larger capesize vessels. The mining group said the port expansion would improve shipping efficiency and reduce freight costs, strengthening its ability to supply overseas customers and Australian alumina refineries. Despite the larger vessels and additional mining capacity, analysts at SEB see limited upside for the capesize market from the investment. The bank noted that much of the new production will replace output from existing mines, leaving a relatively modest increase of around 6m tonnes compared with current Weipa production levels. Any additional volumes are also several years away. SEB further pointed out that shipments from Australia to China involve voyages roughly 3.3 times shorter than those from Guinea, where surging bauxite exports have been a major driver of capesize tonne-mile demand. The bank argued that additional Australian volumes could therefore work against the shift towards longer-haul Guinea-China trades, with the overall impact on dry bulk shipping likely to be negligible. Construction at Kangwinan is scheduled to accelerate in 2027, with the investment including $150m already approved for early works last year. The latest commitment follows Rio Tinto’s September agreement to acquire the neighbouring Aurukun bauxite project from Glencore and Mitsubishi, subject to regulatory approvals. The company intends to integrate the deposit into its longer-term development plans for the region, using existing and planned infrastructure. Bauxite’s growing importance to dry bulk shipping will be reflected at next April’s Geneva Dry , the world’s premier commodities shipping conference, with a standalone Bauxite Blitz session. Scheduled for April 28, the discussion will examine the expanding trade, shifting supply patterns and implications for future capesize demand. Confirmed speakers include Ernst Meyer, president and CEO of Torvald Klaveness, and Robert Haggquist, charterer and decarbonisation lead at South32. Braemar’s Derek Langston will moderate the session. articles.title: Fatigue, fear and the flaws in shipping’s safety data
articles.summary: Seafarer fatigue, mental health and reluctance to report mistakes should become key considerations for marine insurers, banks and investors, according to new research warning that shipping is overlooking significant commercial risks hidden in its own data. The Sustainable Shipping Initiative’s (SSI) From Welfare to...
articles.body: Finance and Insurance Operations Fatigue, fear and the flaws in shipping’s safety data Sam Chambers October 23, 2026 0 853 1 minute read Britannia P&I Britannia P&I Seafarer fatigue, mental health and reluctance to report mistakes should become key considerations for marine insurers, banks and investors, according to new research warning that shipping is overlooking significant commercial risks hidden in its own data. The Sustainable Shipping Initiative’s (SSI) From Welfare to Risk report, published yesterday, examines 68 sources spanning accident investigations, insurance claims, academic studies and seafarer surveys. It finds consistent links between crew wellbeing and safety outcomes, particularly involving fatigue, mental health and psychological safety. Fatigue emerges as the most extensively documented risk factor. The report warns that understaffing and excessive workloads encourage the falsification of rest-hour records, concealing dangerous working conditions from compliance systems. Between a quarter and a third of seafarers do not feel safe raising concerns or reporting mistakes, potentially undermining the accuracy of incident and near-miss reporting. The findings reinforce earlier research covered by Splash . A World Maritime University study published in 2024 found 64.3% of surveyed seafarers adjusted their work/rest records. Another welfare review, reported by Splash last month, found just 49% of seafarers believed their most recent vessel carried sufficient crew to work safely without excessive fatigue. Insurance claims provide further evidence of the financial implications. Gard’s latest crew claims report identifies stress, fatigue and excessive workloads as important factors in onboard injuries, while illness accounts for almost 60% of crew claims. SSI argues insurers can already incorporate welfare indicators into loss-prevention programmes and underwriting discussions, while lenders could include them in borrower monitoring. However, the organisation cautions that current evidence remains insufficient to use welfare indicators as standalone predictors of future claims, insurance premiums or investment performance. The next challenge is connecting existing welfare surveys, accident investigations, port state control findings and insurance claims at vessel and operator level, allowing the industry to quantify how poor crew conditions translate into financial losses. Pictured, a general cargo ship that ran aground five years ago on the rocky coast of the Yailata protected area in Bulgaria. The incident occurred when the ship deviated from its planned course because the second officer on watch fell asleep. articles.title: Icon Energy faces shareholder revolt over dilution
articles.summary: Nasdaq-listed Greek dry bulk owner Icon Energy is facing pressure from a significant shareholder to overhaul its capital structure and board, following accusations that repeated equity issuances have heavily diluted ordinary investors. Canada’s Hampton Financial, which holds 325,000 Icon shares representing...
articles.body: Containers Dry Cargo Europe Icon Energy faces shareholder revolt over dilution Adis Ajdin October 23, 2026 0 366 1 minute read Icon Energy Icon Energy Nasdaq-listed Greek dry bulk owner Icon Energy is facing pressure from a significant shareholder to overhaul its capital structure and board, following accusations that repeated equity issuances have heavily diluted ordinary investors. Canada’s Hampton Financial, which holds 325,000 Icon shares representing approximately 9% of the company, has disclosed a letter sent to Icon’s management demanding changes to its preferred shares, dividend arrangements and corporate governance. Hampton, led by chairman and chief executive Peter Deeb, claims Icon has raised approximately $25m through common share issuances since its 2024 flotation, while ordinary shareholders have suffered substantial losses. The Canadian investment firm has also questioned the treatment of preferred shares held by Icon’s controlling shareholder and chief executive, Ismini Panagiotidi. Hampton is proposing that Icon exchange its outstanding Series A preferred shares for a new instrument with a $20m face value, a fixed 6% cash dividend and conversion rights priced at $5 per ordinary share. It also wants a one-for-one share dividend for existing ordinary shareholders and the appointment of a Hampton-nominated director. The investor argues that these measures would address dilution concerns while preserving Panagiotidi’s control of the business. The proposals have not been accepted or implemented, and the filing does not establish that legal proceedings have commenced. Icon, established in 2023, operates three bulk carriers. The company entered the Nasdaq market in July 2024 and subsequently expanded its fleet through secondhand acquisitions. Its most recent disclosed commercial moves include fixing the 63,668 dwt ultramax Charlie on an index-linked charter extending into 2027 and acquiring a minority investment in two containership projects. The feeder investment, disclosed in June, marked Icon’s first publicly announced move beyond dry bulk shipping.
